27561.q: Which canal did Darius I have completed in Egypt?
a: A canal from the Nile to the Red Sea
A canal from the Nile to the Euphrates
A canal through the Isthmus of Corinth
A canal to the Dead Sea
27561.e: The canal linked the Nile with the Red Sea and so the Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean. Darius had inscriptions put up to commemorate its construction.
27561.m: Darius I had a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea completed.

27562.q: What did the Persian kings mainly use Persepolis for?
a: As a splendid residence for festivals and receptions
As a harbour for the war fleet
27562.e: The Persian kings had palaces and halls built in Persepolis. There they received envoys and held great festivals.
27562.m: Persepolis was a splendid residence of the Persian kings.

27563.q: Who had Persepolis set on fire in 330 BC?
27563.e: After his victory over the Persians, Alexander captured the city. Afterwards the palaces burnt down, perhaps as revenge for the destruction of Athens by the Persians.
27563.m: Alexander the Great had Persepolis burnt down in 330 BC.

27564.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Persepolis?
27564.e: Persepolis lies in south-west Iran, north-east of the city of Shiraz. The ruins are among the best-known sights in the country.
27564.m: The ruins of Persepolis are in Iran.

27565.q: What held up the roof of the great audience hall in Persepolis?
27565.e: The roof of the audience hall rested on 72 columns that were about 20 metres high. Some of them still stand today.
27565.m: The audience hall in Persepolis was a huge hall of columns.

27566.q: What do the famous reliefs on the staircases of Persepolis show?
a: Delegations bringing gifts to the king
27566.e: The reliefs show delegations from many peoples of the empire with gifts such as animals, fabrics and vessels. This shows how large the empire was.
27566.m: The staircase reliefs of Persepolis show gift bearers from many peoples.

27567.q: What can still be seen of Persepolis today?
a: Ruins with columns, stairs and reliefs
Just a hole in the ground
27567.e: The palaces burnt down over 2000 years ago. Columns, stairs, gates and many reliefs have survived. The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27567.m: The ruins of Persepolis are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

27568.q: What does the Greek name “Persepolis” mean?
27568.e: The Greek word “polis” means city. The Persians themselves called the place Parsa.
27568.m: Persepolis means city of the Persians.

27569.q: Where does the word “Samaritan”, used for people who help others, come from?
a: From the region of Samaria in ancient Israel
27569.e: Samaria was the capital and region of the northern kingdom of Israel. In the Bible a “Good Samaritan” helps an injured man, hence the name for helpers.
27569.m: Samaritans are named after the region of Samaria.

27570.q: What happened to many people of the northern kingdom of Israel after it was conquered?
27570.e: The Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom in 722 BC. Part of the population was taken to other areas of the empire.
27570.m: After the conquest many people from Israel were deported.

27571.q: According to the Bible, after the death of which king did the kingdom split into Israel and Judah?
27571.e: According to the Bible, the northern tribes refused to accept Solomon’s son as king. So around 926 BC a northern kingdom and a southern kingdom came into being.
27571.m: According to the Bible, the kingdom split after Solomon’s death.

27572.q: According to the Bible, how many tribes belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel?
27572.e: According to the Bible, ten of the twelve tribes of Israel formed the northern kingdom. Because they disappeared after the conquest, people speak of the “lost tribes”.
27572.m: According to the Bible, ten tribes belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel.

27573.q: What was the capital of the Kingdom of Judah?
27573.e: Jerusalem was the seat of the kings and of the temple. Judah was the smaller southern kingdom.
27573.m: Jerusalem was the capital of the Kingdom of Judah.

27574.q: What is the period called when many Judeans were taken to Babylon?
27574.e: After the fall of Jerusalem, part of Judah’s upper class lived in Babylonia for decades. This period had a strong influence on the Jewish religion.
27574.m: The deportation of the Judeans to Babylon is called the Babylonian Exile.

27575.q: According to the Bible, which family did the kings of Judah come from?
27575.e: According to the Bible, descendants of David ruled in Judah until the end of the kingdom. An inscription from Tel Dan also mentions a “House of David”.
27575.m: The kings of Judah were seen as descendants of David.

27576.q: What did King Hezekiah have built in Jerusalem around 700 BC to supply the city during a siege?
27576.e: The Siloam Tunnel is over 500 metres long and carried spring water into the city. So the people had water even during a siege.
27576.m: King Hezekiah had a water tunnel built in Jerusalem.

27577.q: Which word for people comes from the name Judah?
27577.e: The name of the tribe and Kingdom of Judah became the name for the whole people. The English word “Jews” comes from it.
27577.m: The word “Jews” comes from the name Judah.

27578.q: In which period were the great Pyramids of Giza built?
27578.e: The Pyramids of Giza were built around 2600 to 2500 BC under pharaohs of the 4th Dynasty. This time belongs to the Old Kingdom.
27578.m: The Pyramids of Giza date from the Old Kingdom.

27579.q: Into how many great kingdoms is the history of ancient Egypt usually divided?
27579.e: People distinguish the Old, the Middle and the New Kingdom. In between there were unsettled times when the country fell apart.
27579.m: Ancient Egypt had an Old, a Middle and a New Kingdom.

27580.q: Which crown did the pharaoh wear after Upper and Lower Egypt were united?
27580.e: Upper Egypt had a white crown, Lower Egypt a red one. The pharaoh of the united country wore both together as a double crown.
27580.m: The double crown showed that the pharaoh ruled all of Egypt.

27581.q: Which weapon of war did the Egyptians only learn about from foreigners from western Asia?
27581.e: Foreign rulers from western Asia brought horses and chariots to Egypt. After that the pharaohs also used chariots in war.
27581.m: Foreigners from western Asia brought the chariot to Egypt.

27582.q: Which city was the most important religious centre of Egypt in the New Kingdom?
27582.e: Thebes, today’s Luxor, was the city of the god Amun. Huge temples were built there, and the royal tombs on the west bank.
27582.m: Thebes was the religious heart of Egypt in the New Kingdom.

27583.q: What do you call a series of rulers who come from the same family?
27583.e: The pharaohs are divided into dynasties. Often a son followed his father onto the throne.
27583.m: Rulers from the same family form a dynasty.

27584.q: After the death of which ruler did the Ptolemaic period begin in Egypt?
27584.e: Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BC. After his death his general Ptolemy took over the country and founded his own dynasty.
27584.m: The Ptolemies followed Alexander the Great.

27585.q: Which part of the country is called Lower Egypt?
a: The Nile Delta in the north
The Nile Valley in the south
27585.e: The Nile flows from south to north. That is why the area downstream, the delta on the Mediterranean, is called Lower Egypt.
27585.m: Lower Egypt is the Nile Delta in the north.

a: She was a woman who ruled as pharaoh
She was the first queen of Rome
27586.e: Hatshepsut had herself crowned pharaoh and ruled for about 20 years. Women on the pharaoh’s throne were very rare.
27586.m: Hatshepsut was a woman who ruled as pharaoh.

27587.q: Roughly how long did Hatshepsut rule?
27587.e: Hatshepsut ruled for about 20 years in the 15th century BC. Her reign is seen as peaceful and prosperous.

27588.q: How is Hatshepsut’s famous temple built?
a: In several terraces in front of a cliff
27588.e: The temple rises in several wide terraces towards the cliffs. It lies on the west bank of the Nile near today’s Luxor.
27588.m: Hatshepsut’s temple is a terraced temple.

27589.q: What did a famous trade expedition sent by Hatshepsut bring back, among other things?
27589.e: Hatshepsut sent ships to the land of Punt on the Red Sea. They brought back frankincense, myrrh, ebony and exotic animals.
27589.m: Hatshepsut’s ships brought frankincense and myrrh to Egypt.

27590.q: What happened to many of Hatshepsut’s statues and pictures long after her death?
a: They were destroyed or her name was removed
They were sunk in the sea
27590.e: Later, many statues of Hatshepsut were smashed and her name was removed from inscriptions. This was meant to make her vanish from memory.
27590.m: Later, people tried to erase Hatshepsut from history.

a: In the Valley of the Kings
27591.e: Hatshepsut had a rock tomb made for herself in the Valley of the Kings near Luxor. The pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried there.
27591.m: Hatshepsut’s tomb is in the Valley of the Kings.

27592.q: Which male sign of kingship does Hatshepsut wear on many statues?
27592.e: Pharaohs wore a false beard at ceremonies. Hatshepsut had herself shown with one to display her role as king.
27592.m: Hatshepsut had herself shown with the royal beard.

27593.q: In which country did Hatshepsut rule?
27593.e: Hatshepsut was a pharaoh in ancient Egypt. She ruled from the Nile valley in the 15th century BC.

27594.q: Which god did Akhenaten place above all other gods?
a: Osiris, the god of the dead
27594.e: Akhenaten worshipped almost only Aten, shown as a sun disc with rays ending in hands. Other cults, especially that of Amun, were pushed back.
27594.m: Akhenaten worshipped above all the sun god Aten.

27595.q: In which country did Akhenaten rule?
27595.e: Akhenaten was a pharaoh in ancient Egypt. He ruled in the 14th century BC.
27595.m: Akhenaten was a pharaoh in Egypt.

27596.q: What did Akhenaten have newly built for his god Aten?
27596.e: Akhenaten founded the city of Akhetaten, “Horizon of the Aten”. Today the place is called Amarna.
27596.m: Akhenaten built a new capital for Aten.

27597.q: According to DNA tests, which famous pharaoh is thought to be Akhenaten’s son?
27597.e: Genetic tests on the mummies suggest that Akhenaten was Tutankhamun’s father. Tutankhamun returned to the worship of Amun.
27597.m: Tutankhamun was probably a son of Akhenaten.

27598.q: What was new about the art from Akhenaten’s time?
a: It had no colours at all
27598.e: Artists showed people in a more lifelike way and even showed family scenes of the royal family. This style is called Amarna art.
27598.m: Under Akhenaten, art became more natural.

27599.q: In which city can you see the famous bust of Nefertiti today?
27599.e: The painted bust is in the Neues Museum on Museum Island in Berlin. It is one of the best-known works of art in the world.
27599.m: The bust of Nefertiti is in Berlin.

27600.q: What is the famous bust of Nefertiti made of?
27600.e: The bust is made of limestone with a painted layer of plaster. A German team found it in 1912 in a sculptor’s workshop in Amarna.
27600.m: The bust of Nefertiti is made of painted limestone.

27601.q: What does the name Nefertiti mean?
27601.e: Translated, the name Nefertiti means “The beautiful one has come”. She was Akhenaten’s chief wife.
27601.m: Nefertiti means “The beautiful one has come”.

27602.q: How did Ramesses II have his great battle against the Hittites shown, even though it probably ended in a draw?
27602.e: Ramesses II had the Battle of Kadesh shown on many temple walls as a glorious victory. In truth, neither side won.
27602.m: Ramesses II presented his battle as a great victory.

27603.q: Why is Ramesses II also called “Ramesses the Great”?
a: He ruled for a long time and had many huge buildings built
He was over two metres tall
27603.e: Ramesses II ruled for about 66 years. He had many temples and huge statues of himself built, for example at Abu Simbel.
27603.m: Ramesses II was one of the most powerful pharaohs.

27604.q: Roughly how old did Ramesses II live to be, according to estimates?
27604.e: Ramesses II came to the throne young and ruled for a very long time. Experts estimate that he died at about 90, a very great age for that time.
27604.m: Ramesses II lived to a very old age for his time.

27605.q: On which river did the kingdom of Ramesses II lie?
27605.e: Ancient Egypt lay along the Nile. The river brought water and fertile mud for the fields.
27605.m: The kingdom of the pharaohs lay on the Nile.

27606.q: Why were the temples of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel moved to a higher place in the 1960s?
a: A new reservoir would have flooded them
An earthquake had knocked them over
They were to go to a museum in Europe
The desert sand had covered them
27606.e: A huge lake was created for the Aswan Dam. The temples were sawn into blocks and rebuilt higher up.
27606.m: The temples of Abu Simbel were saved from the reservoir.

27607.q: To which city was the mummy of Ramesses II flown for treatment in 1976?
27607.e: The mummy was attacked by a fungus and was examined and treated in Paris. The often-told story that it was given a passport for the trip is not true.
27607.m: The mummy of Ramesses II travelled to Paris in 1976.

27608.q: For whom did Ramesses II have a second temple built next to his own at Abu Simbel?
a: His enemy, the king of the Hittites
27608.e: The smaller temple at Abu Simbel is dedicated to Nefertari and the goddess Hathor. Ramesses showed how much he honoured his wife.
27608.m: At Abu Simbel there is also a temple for Nefertari.

27609.q: How was the body of Ramesses II preserved for eternity after his death?
a: It was thrown into the sea
27609.e: The Egyptians dried the body and wrapped it in linen bandages. The mummy of Ramesses II still exists today.
27609.m: The mummy of Ramesses II still exists today.

27610.q: Where is the Valley of the Kings?
a: On the west bank of the Nile near Luxor
On the east bank of the Nile near Cairo
In the Nile Delta near Alexandria
On the Red Sea near Hurghada
27610.e: The valley lies in the hills opposite Luxor, the ancient city of Thebes. For the Egyptians, the land of the dead lay in the west, where the sun sets.
27610.m: The Valley of the Kings is on the west bank near Luxor.

27611.q: Who was mainly buried in the Valley of the Queens?
a: Wives and children of the pharaohs
The workers who built the tombs
27611.e: In the Valley of the Queens on the west bank at Luxor there are tombs of the pharaohs’ wives and children. It is only a few kilometres from the Valley of the Kings.
27611.m: Queens and princes rest in the Valley of the Queens.

27612.q: In which year was Tutankhamun’s tomb discovered?
27612.e: In November 1922 the excavators came across the steps leading to the tomb. The find made headlines around the world.

27613.q: Why was Tutankhamun’s tomb a sensation?
a: It was almost untouched and full of treasures
It was the biggest tomb in Egypt
It was on a mountain top
27613.e: Almost all royal tombs had already been robbed in ancient times. Tutankhamun’s tomb KV62, however, was almost untouched. KV stands for Kings’ Valley.
27613.m: Tutankhamun’s tomb was almost untouched and full of treasures.

27614.q: Why were the pharaohs of the New Kingdom buried in hidden rock tombs instead of pyramids?
a: To protect them from tomb robbers
Because the Nile flooded the pyramids
27614.e: Pyramids could be seen from far away and nearly all of them were robbed. The tombs cut deep into the rock were meant to stay better hidden.
27614.m: Rock tombs were meant to protect the pharaohs from tomb robbers.

27615.q: From which period do most of the tombs in the Valley of the Kings date?
27615.e: From about 1500 to 1070 BC the pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried here. They include rulers of the 18th to 20th dynasties.
27615.m: Pharaohs of the New Kingdom rest in the Valley of the Kings.

27616.q: Who built and painted the tombs in the Valley of the Kings?
a: Craftsmen who lived in their own village
27616.e: Stonemasons, painters and scribes lived with their families in the village of Deir el-Medina. They were well-trained experts and were paid in grain.
27616.m: Craftsmen from Deir el-Medina created the royal tombs.

27617.q: What shape is the mountain peak above the Valley of the Kings?
a: It looks like a lion lying down
It is shaped like a ring
27617.e: The peak is called el-Qurn and looks like a natural pyramid. Perhaps this is one reason why the valley was chosen as the burial ground of the pharaohs.
27617.m: A pyramid-shaped peak rises above the Valley of the Kings.

27618.q: Which famous pharaoh had the temples of Abu Simbel built?
27618.e: Ramesses II had the rock temples built around 1260 BC. In front of the great temple sit four huge statues of him.
27618.m: Abu Simbel was built by Ramesses II.

27619.q: What kind of rock were the temples of Abu Simbel carved from?
27619.e: The temples were carved directly out of a sandstone hill by the Nile. Sandstone is easy to work and was often used in Upper Egypt.
27619.m: The temples of Abu Simbel are made of sandstone.

27620.q: Why were the temples of Abu Simbel taken apart and rebuilt higher up in the 20th century?
a: Otherwise a reservoir would have flooded them
They were in the way of a road
The sand threatened to bury them
27620.e: A huge reservoir was created for the new Aswan Dam on the Nile. So that the temples would not sink, they were taken apart and rebuilt in a higher place.
27620.m: Abu Simbel was saved from the water of a reservoir.

27621.q: Which organisation led the rescue of the temples of Abu Simbel?
27621.e: UNESCO called on many countries to help with the rescue. Today the temples are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27621.m: UNESCO helped to save Abu Simbel.

27622.q: Which Swiss city did the explorer come from who rediscovered Abu Simbel for Europe in 1813?
27622.e: Johann Ludwig Burckhardt from Basel travelled through the Orient in disguise. In 1813 he saw the heads of the statues sticking out of the sand.
27622.m: An explorer from Basel rediscovered Abu Simbel in 1813.

27623.q: By roughly how many metres were the temples of Abu Simbel raised when they were rescued?
27623.e: The temples were taken apart and rebuilt about 65 metres higher and a little further inland. Artificial hills were built over them.
27623.m: The temples of Abu Simbel now stand about 65 metres higher.

27624.q: How many rock temples make up Abu Simbel?
27624.e: There is a large temple and a small one. Both lie side by side on the bank of the Nile.
27624.m: Abu Simbel consists of two rock temples.

27625.q: In which modern city is the Karnak temple?
27625.e: The temple complex lies on the east bank of the Nile in today’s Luxor. In ancient times it belonged to the city of Thebes.
27625.m: The Karnak temple is in Luxor.

27626.q: What did the ancient Egyptians use the Karnak temple for?
27626.e: Karnak was a huge sanctuary, above all for the god Amun-Ra. Priests made offerings there every day and held great festivals.
27626.m: The Karnak temple was a sanctuary for the gods.

27627.q: What are the columns in the great hall of columns at Karnak decorated with?
27627.e: The 134 mighty columns are covered all over with carved hieroglyphs and pictures. They show gods and pharaohs.
27627.m: The columns of Karnak are full of hieroglyphs.

27628.q: What linked the Karnak temple with the Luxor temple?
27628.e: A processional road almost three kilometres long was lined with sphinxes. It has been uncovered in recent years.
27628.m: An avenue of sphinxes leads from Karnak to the Luxor temple.

27629.q: Which body of water belongs to the temple complex of Karnak?
27629.e: There is an artificial sacred lake in the complex. Priests purified themselves there before the rituals.
27629.m: The Karnak temple has a sacred lake.

27630.q: Roughly how long did building work go on at the Karnak temple complex?
27630.e: From the Middle Kingdom to the Ptolemaic period, many pharaohs added new buildings. This created one of the largest temple complexes in the world.
27630.m: Pharaohs built at the Karnak temple for about 2000 years.

27631.q: What are the tall, pointed stone pillars made from a single piece that stood in front of Egyptian temples such as Karnak called?
27631.e: An obelisk is a tall, four-sided pillar with a point at the top. Obelisks still stand at Karnak today, for example one of Hatshepsut’s.
27631.m: Obelisks stood in front of Egyptian temples.

27632.q: Roughly how big is the Rosetta Stone?
a: As tall as a church tower
27632.e: The stone is a good metre tall and weighs about 760 kilograms. It is only a fragment of a larger stone slab.
27632.m: The Rosetta Stone is a good metre tall.

27633.q: About how many years ago was the Rosetta Stone found?
27633.e: The stone was found in 1799, so a good 200 years ago. But it was inscribed as early as 196 BC.
27633.m: The Rosetta Stone was found a good 200 years ago.

27634.q: During which event was the Rosetta Stone found?
a: During the building of the Suez Canal
27634.e: In 1798 Napoleon went to Egypt with soldiers and many scholars. During this, his men came across the stone.
27634.m: The Rosetta Stone was discovered during Napoleon’s campaign.

27635.q: Which script on the Rosetta Stone could scholars already read at that time?
27635.e: Scholars could read Ancient Greek. They compared this version with the two Egyptian scripts. The find had been reported in 1799 by the French officer Pierre-François Bouchard.
27635.m: The Greek text on the Rosetta Stone could be read.

27636.q: What does the text on the Rosetta Stone say?
a: A decree by priests honouring a king
27636.e: The text is a decree by priests from the year 196 BC. It honours the young king Ptolemy V.
27636.m: The Rosetta Stone contains a decree by priests.

27637.q: What is the Rosetta Stone made of?
27637.e: The stone is made of granodiorite, a hard, dark rock. For a long time it was thought to be basalt.
27637.m: The Rosetta Stone is made of hard, dark rock.

27638.q: Where does the Rosetta Stone get its name from?
a: From a town in the Nile Delta
From the person who found it
27638.e: Rosetta is the European name of the town of Rashid on a branch of the Nile. The stone was discovered near it.
27638.m: Rosetta is a town in the Nile Delta.

27639.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone so important for research?
a: It shows the same text in three scripts
It is the oldest stone in the world
27639.e: Because the same content appears three times, the known text could be compared with the unknown signs. This made it the key to the hieroglyphs.
27639.m: The Rosetta Stone was the key to the hieroglyphs.

27640.q: Which country did Jean-François Champollion come from?
27640.e: Champollion was born in 1790 in Figeac in southern France. Even as a child he learned many ancient languages.

27641.q: Which famous stone helped Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs?
27641.e: The Rosetta Stone has the same text in hieroglyphs, in another Egyptian script and in Greek. With it, Champollion made his breakthrough in 1822.
27641.m: The Rosetta Stone was the key to the hieroglyphs.

27642.q: Which names are written inside an oval frame in hieroglyphic texts?
27642.e: Royal names such as Ptolemy and Cleopatra are written in an oval. By comparing these names, Champollion worked out which sounds individual signs stand for.
27642.m: Royal names are written in an oval frame.

27643.q: Which language on the Rosetta Stone could scholars already read?
27643.e: The Greek text on the stone could be understood. Because the hieroglyphs give the same content, they could be compared.
27643.m: The Greek text helped to decipher the hieroglyphs.

27644.q: What does it mean to decipher an ancient script?
a: To find out what the signs mean
To carve a script in stone
To write a script more beautifully
27644.e: Someone who deciphers a script finds out what the signs stand for. Champollion managed this with the hieroglyphs in 1822.
27644.m: Deciphering means finding out the meaning of signs.

27645.q: What did Champollion realise about the hieroglyphs?
a: Some are sound signs and some are picture signs
They are only pictures without sounds
They are a secret code of the Greeks
27645.e: Many hieroglyphs stand for sounds, others for whole words or act as signs that show the meaning. This mixture was the most important discovery.
27645.m: Hieroglyphs combine sound signs and picture signs.

27646.q: Which country did Champollion travel to so he could see hieroglyphs on temples for himself?
27646.e: In 1828 and 1829 Champollion travelled through Egypt. He read many inscriptions there and was able to confirm his decipherment.

27647.q: From which plant did the Egyptians make their writing material?
a: From a marsh plant on the Nile
From the bark of oak trees
27647.e: The papyrus plant is a sedge that grew in marshes along the Nile. It was also used to make boats, ropes and mats.
27647.m: Papyrus grows as a marsh plant on the Nile.

27648.q: How was papyrus made as a writing material?
a: Strips of the pith were laid crosswise and pressed
Wood was boiled into a pulp and dried
Animal skin was stretched and scraped
Clay was fired into thin tablets
27648.e: The pith of the stems was cut into thin strips. Two layers placed crosswise on top of each other were pressed and dried.
27648.m: Papyrus is made of pressed plant strips laid crosswise.

27649.q: What is in the famous Rhind Papyrus from Egypt?
27649.e: The Rhind Papyrus dates from around 1550 BC. It shows how scribes calculated areas, portions of bread and fractions.
27649.m: The Rhind Papyrus is an ancient Egyptian maths book.

27650.q: In what form were long papyrus texts usually kept?
27650.e: Single sheets were glued together and rolled up. Some scrolls were many metres long.
27650.m: Long texts on papyrus were rolled up.

27651.q: Apart from black, which ink colour did Egyptian scribes use especially often?
27651.e: Black ink was made from soot, red from ochre. Red was used for headings and the beginnings of sections.
27651.m: Besides black, the Egyptians often wrote in red ink.

27652.q: Why have many papyri in Egypt survived for thousands of years?
a: Because of the very dry climate
Because of a protective coat of gold
Because they lay in the Nile
Because they were made of stone
27652.e: Papyrus rots quickly when it is damp. But in the dry desert sand and in tombs, many texts lasted a very long time.
27652.m: The dry climate preserved many papyri.

27653.q: For a long time, what did the Egyptians write on papyrus with?
27653.e: The end of a rush stem was chewed soft so that it worked like a brush. The sharpened reed pen only came later.
27653.m: The Egyptians wrote with a rush as if with a brush.

27654.q: What is the Egyptian Book of the Dead?
a: A collection of spells for the afterlife
A law book of the pharaohs
27654.e: The spells were meant to help the dead survive dangers in the afterlife. They were usually written on papyrus and placed in the tomb.
27654.m: The Book of the Dead contains magic spells for the afterlife.

27655.q: What did the Egyptians usually write the spells of the Book of the Dead on?
27655.e: Papyrus was made from a plant on the Nile. The Book of the Dead scrolls were placed in the tombs of the dead.
27655.m: The Book of the Dead was written on papyrus.

27656.q: At the judgement of the dead, what is the heart of the dead person weighed against?
27656.e: The feather stands for Maat, truth and justice. If the heart was not heavier, the dead person could enter the afterlife.
27656.m: At the judgement of the dead, the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat.

27657.q: Which jackal-headed god works the scales at the judgement of the dead?
27657.e: Anubis was the god of mummification and the companion of the dead. In many pictures in the Book of the Dead he checks the scales.
27657.m: Anubis works the scales at the judgement of the dead.

27658.q: What did the dead person have to declare before the gods at the judgement of the dead?
a: That he had done nothing evil
That he had been very rich
That he had won many wars
That he had drawn all the gods
27658.e: Before the judges of the dead, the dead person listed many wrongdoings and declared that he had not committed them. In this way he wanted to show that he had led a just life.
27658.m: At the judgement of the dead, the dead person declared his innocence.

27659.q: According to the Book of the Dead, what happened to the heart of someone who failed the judgement of the dead?
a: It was thrown into the Nile
It was given to the pharaoh
27659.e: A monster that was part crocodile, part lion and part hippopotamus devoured the heart. This meant the dead person could not reach the afterlife.
27659.m: The heart of a guilty person was eaten by a monster.

27661.q: Which god presides over the judgement of the dead?
27661.e: Osiris is the ruler of the underworld. He sits on the throne and welcomes the just dead.
27661.m: Osiris leads the judgement of the dead.

27662.q: How do scribes sit on many ancient Egyptian statues?
a: Cross-legged with papyrus on their knees
On a throne with a crown
27662.e: Many statues show scribes sitting cross-legged. A papyrus scroll lies on their knees. The most famous of these figures is in the Louvre in Paris.
27662.m: Scribes were often shown sitting cross-legged with papyrus.

27663.q: Which ibis-headed god was the protector of scribes?
27663.e: Thoth was the god of wisdom, the moon and writing. Before starting work, scribes offered him a drop of water.
27663.m: Thoth was the god of writing and of scribes.

27664.q: What was an Egyptian scribe’s most important tool?
a: A wax tablet with a stylus
27664.e: The palette was a long wooden case with hollows for ink and a slot for the rushes. It was often placed in the tomb as a sign of the profession.
27664.m: The writing palette was the typical tool of scribes.

27665.q: Where were scribes usually trained in ancient Egypt?
a: In schools at temples and palaces
27665.e: Young scribes studied for years at writing schools in temples and at the pharaoh’s court. Such a temple school was called a House of Life.
27665.m: Scribes learned in schools at temples and palaces.

27667.q: What job did scribes often do in ancient Egypt?
27667.e: Scribes recorded taxes, counted cattle and supplies and kept lists. Without them the state would not have worked.
27667.m: Scribes kept written records of taxes and supplies.

27668.q: Why was being a scribe seen as a particularly good job in Egypt?
a: Scribes were respected and did not have to do hard work
Scribes paid twice as much tax
Scribes never had to learn anything
27668.e: Only a few people could read and write. Scribes were therefore highly respected and did not have to toil in the fields or on building sites. Old teaching texts such as the Satire of the Trades therefore advised children to become scribes.
27668.m: Scribes were respected in ancient Egypt.

27669.q: Which language did Cleopatra’s ruling family, which originally came from Macedonia, speak?
27669.e: Cleopatra’s family was descended from a general of Alexander the Great. Greek was therefore spoken at the court in Alexandria.

27670.q: In which city did Cleopatra VII live and rule?
27670.e: Alexandria on the Mediterranean was the capital of the Ptolemies. The city was famous for its lighthouse and its library.

27671.q: Which Roman general was the father of Cleopatra’s son Caesarion?
27671.e: Cleopatra allied herself with Caesar in 48 BC. Their son was given the nickname Caesarion, “little Caesar”.
27671.m: Caesarion was the son of Cleopatra and Caesar.

27672.q: After Caesar’s death, which Roman was Cleopatra allied with and in a relationship with?
27672.e: After Caesar was murdered, Mark Antony became her partner. They had three children together.
27672.m: Cleopatra allied herself with Mark Antony.

27673.q: Who defeated Cleopatra and Mark Antony in 31 BC?
27673.e: Octavian’s fleet won the sea battle of Actium. Later, as Augustus, he became the first Roman emperor.
27673.m: Octavian defeated Cleopatra and Mark Antony.

27674.q: According to tradition, how did Cleopatra die?
27674.e: Ancient writers report that she let a poisonous snake bite her. Whether this really happened is not certain.
27674.m: According to tradition, Cleopatra died from a snakebite.

27675.q: What did Egypt become after Cleopatra’s death in 30 BC?
27675.e: Octavian, the later Emperor Augustus, took possession of Egypt. The country became a province of the Roman Empire.

27676.q: According to Plutarch, what could Cleopatra do as the first of her ruling family?
27676.e: The Ptolemies spoke Greek. According to the writer Plutarch, Cleopatra was the first to also learn Egyptian and many other languages.
27676.m: Cleopatra was the first Ptolemy to speak Egyptian.

27677.e: Cleopatra was born in 69 BC and died in 30 BC. She lived in the late period of the Roman Republic.
27677.m: Cleopatra lived in the 1st century BC.

27678.q: How did the Minoans on Crete become rich and powerful?
a: Through sea trade with their ships
Through gold mines in the Alps
27678.e: The Minoans traded with Egypt, Cyprus and other islands. Greek writers said that King Minos ruled the Aegean with his fleet.
27678.m: The Minoans were a sea power.

27679.q: Which mysterious find from Crete has stamped signs arranged in a spiral?
27679.e: The clay disc was found in 1908 in the palace of Phaistos. Its signs were pressed in with stamps and have still not been explained.
27679.m: The Phaistos Disc is one of the great mysteries of archaeology.

27680.q: Which city was the largest centre of Minoan culture?
27680.e: The palace of Knossos was the largest of the Minoan palaces, with over a thousand rooms. It lies near today’s Heraklion.
27680.m: Knossos was the most important palace of the Minoans.

27681.q: What is still a mystery about the Minoan script Linear A?
a: Only a single sign has been found
It can only be read from below
27681.e: Thanks to the later script Linear B, many signs can roughly be read. But the language behind them is still not understood today.
27681.m: The language of Linear A has not yet been deciphered.

27682.q: According to legend, which mythical creature lived in the labyrinth beneath the palace of the king of Crete?
27682.e: In the legend, the Minotaur was half man and half bull. Many people link the winding palace of Knossos with the labyrinth.
27682.m: According to legend, the Minotaur lived in the labyrinth of Crete.

27683.q: Which very modern feature for the Bronze Age did Minoan palaces have?
27683.e: At Knossos, clay pipes for water and channels for waste water were found. This shows how advanced the builders were.
27683.m: The Minoans already had water pipes.

27684.q: On which island did a huge volcano erupt in the Bronze Age, also badly affecting the Minoan world?
27684.e: The volcano of Santorini (Thera) exploded in the 2nd millennium BC. Ash and tidal waves also damaged Crete, which is only about 110 km away.
27684.m: The eruption of Santorini was a disaster for the Aegean.

27685.q: What is the famous entrance gate of the citadel of Mycenae called?
27685.e: Above the gate are two stone lions on either side of a column. It is one of the oldest large reliefs in Europe.
27685.m: The Lion Gate is the landmark of Mycenae.

27686.q: In which language did the Mycenaeans write on their clay tablets?
a: In an early form of Greek
27686.e: The Mycenaeans used the script Linear B mainly to write lists of supplies. It was deciphered in 1952 and shows the oldest known Greek.
27686.m: The Mycenaeans already wrote in Greek.

27687.q: What are the huge stone walls of Mycenae called, which legend said were built by giants?
27687.e: The blocks are so big that later Greeks believed only the one-eyed giants could have piled them up. That is where the name comes from.
27687.m: The mighty walls of Mycenae are called Cyclopean walls.

27688.q: Roughly when did Mycenaean culture flourish?
27688.e: Mycenaean culture belongs to the late Bronze Age. Around 1200 BC many of its palaces were destroyed, and after that it fell apart.
27688.m: Mycenaean culture flourished in the late Bronze Age.

27689.q: What was the so-called “Treasury of Atreus” in Mycenae really?
27689.e: It is a large tholos tomb with a dome made of rings of stone. The name is misleading, because it was a burial place for rulers.
27689.m: The Treasury of Atreus is really a domed tomb.

27690.q: Which poet tells of heroes from the time of the Mycenaeans in the Iliad?
27690.e: Homer’s Iliad tells of the Trojan War. The leader of the Greeks in it is Agamemnon, king of Mycenae.
27690.m: In the Iliad, Homer tells of Mycenaean heroes.

27691.q: On which peninsula is the citadel of Mycenae?
27691.e: Mycenae lies in the region of Argolis in the north-east of the Peloponnese. From there, important routes could be controlled.

27692.q: According to legend, to which goddess did the Trojan prince Paris award the golden apple?
27692.e: In return, Aphrodite promised him the most beautiful woman in the world. Hera and Athena therefore became enemies of Troy.
27692.m: The Judgement of Paris was the beginning of Troy’s misfortune.

27693.q: Which king was Helen married to?
27693.e: Helen was the wife of the Spartan king Menelaus. He called on the Greeks to go to war for revenge.
27693.m: Helen was the wife of Menelaus.

27694.q: According to legend, how long did the Trojan War last?
27694.e: According to legend, the Greeks besieged Troy for ten years. Only a trick finally decided the war.
27694.m: In the legend, the Trojan War lasted ten years.

27695.q: According to legend, which Trojan fled from the burning city and was later seen as the ancestor of the Romans?
27695.e: The Roman poet Virgil tells of his escape to Italy in the Aeneid. In this way the Romans linked their origins with Troy.
27695.m: Aeneas links the legend of Troy with Rome.

27696.q: According to legend, who was king of Troy during the war?
27696.e: Priam was the old king of Troy and the father of many sons. He lived to see the fall of his city.
27696.m: Priam was the king of Troy.

27697.q: According to legend, which king of Mycenae led the Greek army against Troy?
27697.e: Agamemnon was the brother of Menelaus and commander-in-chief of the Greeks. He was the most powerful of the Greek kings.
27697.m: Agamemnon was the leader of the Greeks at Troy.

27698.q: On which strait did the city of Troy lie?
27698.e: Troy lay near the entrance to the Dardanelles, which link the Aegean Sea with the Sea of Marmara. This position was important for trade and power.
27698.m: Troy controlled the route through the Dardanelles.

27699.q: According to legend, on which part of his body could the hero Achilles be wounded?
a: On the back of his neck
27699.e: As a baby, his mother dipped him in the River Styx, holding him by the heel. Later a deadly arrow struck him there.
27699.m: An Achilles heel is a weak spot.

27700.q: Which one-eyed giant does Odysseus outwit in the Odyssey?
27700.e: Odysseus and his companions are trapped in a cave by the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus blinds him and escapes with his men hidden under the sheep.

a: Poem about Ilion, that is Troy
Song of the anger of the gods
Book of the heroes of Sparta
27701.e: Ilion was another name for the city of Troy. So the Iliad is the poem about Troy.
27701.m: The name Iliad comes from Ilion, the other name for Troy.

27702.q: Roughly speaking, with which word does the Iliad begin: “Sing, goddess, the ... of Achilles”?
27702.e: The rage of Achilles is the main theme of the Iliad. Because he feels insulted, he at first withdraws from the fighting.
27702.m: The Iliad begins with the rage of Achilles.

27703.q: What do you call a long heroic poem in verse such as the Iliad?
27703.e: An epic tells the deeds of heroes and gods in many lines of verse. The Iliad and the Odyssey are seen as the oldest epics in Europe.

27704.q: Athena disguises herself as which old friend of Odysseus in order to help his son?
27704.e: In the Odyssey, Athena advises young Telemachus in the form of Mentor. That is why an experienced adviser is called a mentor today.
27704.m: The word mentor comes from the Odyssey.

27706.q: Why did Odysseus have himself tied to the mast of his ship?
a: To hear the Sirens’ song without following them
So as not to fall into the sea in a storm
Because he wanted to punish his companions
27706.e: The Sirens lured sailors to their doom with their singing. Odysseus wanted to hear them. His companions blocked their ears with wax and tied him tight.
27706.m: Odysseus had himself tied to the mast because of the Sirens.

27708.q: Who had more soldiers at the Battle of Marathon?
a: Both armies were the same size
27708.e: The Persian army was clearly bigger than the Athenian one. Even so, the Athenians won the battle.
27708.m: At Marathon, the Athenians beat a much larger force.

27709.q: Who won the Battle of Marathon?
27709.e: The Athenians, with a small force of helpers, defeated the larger Persian army. This ended the first Persian attack on Athens in failure.
27709.m: At Marathon, the Athenians defeated the Persians.

27710.q: Which running race is named after the Battle of Marathon?
27710.e: According to a legend, a messenger ran from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory. The marathon over about 42 kilometres recalls this.
27710.m: The marathon recalls the Battle of Marathon.

27711.q: Why did the Spartans only arrive after the Battle of Marathon?
a: They were celebrating a religious festival
27711.e: The Spartans did not want to set out until after the full moon, because a sacred festival was taking place. When they arrived, the battle was already over.
27711.m: Because of a festival, the Spartans arrived too late at Marathon.

27712.q: Who lost far more soldiers at the Battle of Marathon?
27712.e: According to Herodotus, only about 200 Athenians fell, but about 6400 Persians. For Athens it was a great victory.
27712.m: At Marathon, far more Persians fell than Athenians.

27714.q: Why did the Persian king attack Athens?
a: Athens had helped Greeks against Persia
Athens had invited the king to a festival
27714.e: Greek cities in Asia Minor fought back against the Persians. Athens sent them ships to help, and the Persian king wanted to punish Athens for it.
27714.m: Athens had supported Greeks against the Persians.

27715.q: How did the Persian army get to Marathon?
a: In horse-drawn carts over a bridge to Athens
27715.e: The Persians crossed the Aegean with a large fleet and landed in the bay of Marathon north of Athens.
27715.m: The Persians came to Marathon by ship.

27716.q: Which Spartan king defended the pass of Thermopylae against the Persians?
27716.e: Leonidas led a Greek army to hold up the Persians at the narrow pass. He fell in the battle.
27716.m: Leonidas died a hero at Thermopylae.

27717.q: According to tradition, how many Spartans fought at Thermopylae?
27717.e: Tradition speaks of 300 full Spartan citizens. Several thousand warriors from other Greek cities fought with them.
27717.m: The 300 Spartans of Thermopylae are still famous today.

27718.q: Which Persian Great King led the army at Thermopylae?
27718.e: Xerxes I marched against Greece with a huge army and a large fleet. He wanted to avenge his father’s defeat.
27718.m: Xerxes I led the great Persian campaign against Greece.

27719.q: What does the name “Thermopylae” mean in translation?
27719.e: The name comes from hot sulphur springs nearby. “Pylai” means “gates” in Greek.

27720.q: How did the Persians get behind the Greeks at Thermopylae?
a: Along a mountain path shown to them by a traitor
Over a bridge made of boats
27720.e: A Greek called Ephialtes showed the Persians a path over the mountains. This let them get round the defenders.
27720.m: Betrayal brought the Persians success at Thermopylae.

27721.q: How did the Battle of Thermopylae end?
a: With a defeat for the Greeks
With a clear victory for the Greeks
With the death of the Persian king
27721.e: The Greek rearguard was completely wiped out. Even so, their resistance became a model of bravery.

27722.q: Why did the Greeks choose the pass of Thermopylae for their defence?
a: The narrow place weakened the big Persian army
There was a lot of gold there
The Persians were afraid of hot springs
27722.e: Between the mountains and the sea the way was very narrow. There, a few Greeks could hold up a huge army for a long time.
27722.m: In the narrow pass, a few Greeks could hold up many Persians.

27723.q: What answer is the Spartan king said to have given when the Persians demanded that the Greeks hand over their weapons?
27723.e: The words “Molon labe” mean roughly “Come and take them”. They were recorded by Plutarch.
27723.m: “Molon labe” is a famous saying of defiance.

27724.q: Who won the sea battle of Salamis?
27724.e: In 480 BC the Greek fleet defeated the much larger Persian fleet. It was a turning point of the Persian Wars.
27724.m: At Salamis, the Greeks defeated the Persians.

27725.q: What did Athens have built before the Battle of Salamis to defend itself against the Persians?
a: A wall around all of Greece
27725.e: On the advice of the politician Themistocles, Athens built many warships. With this fleet the Greeks won at Salamis.
27725.m: Athens built a large fleet against the Persians.

27726.q: Which type of ship with three rows of rowers fought at Salamis?
27726.e: A trireme had about 170 rowers on three levels. With a ram at the bow it could sink enemy ships.
27726.m: The trireme was the warship of the Greeks.

27727.q: Where is the island of Salamis, after which the sea battle is named?
a: In the Saronic Gulf near Athens
Off the coast of Asia Minor
In the north of the Adriatic
27727.e: Salamis lies only a few kilometres off Piraeus, the port of Athens. The narrow strait between the island and the mainland became the battlefield.
27727.m: Salamis is very close to Athens.

27728.q: Why was the narrow strait at Salamis good for the Greeks?
a: The large Persian fleet could not spread out
The current pushed the Greeks forward
27728.e: In the narrow bay, the many Persian ships got in each other’s way. The smaller Greek fleet could attack more easily.
27728.m: In the narrow strait, the large Persian fleet was at a disadvantage.

27729.q: What did most of the people of Athens do before the sea battle of Salamis?
27729.e: Women, children and old people were taken to Salamis and Troezen. The Persians occupied the empty city and laid it waste.
27729.m: Athens was evacuated before Salamis and laid waste by the Persians.

27730.q: Which metal helped Athens to pay for its large fleet?
27730.e: A rich vein of silver was found near Athens. With the silver, Athens built about 200 warships.

27731.q: What did the defeat at Salamis mean for the Persian king?
a: He withdrew to Asia with part of his army
He made an alliance with Athens
27731.e: After losing many ships, the king returned to Asia Minor. The rest of the land army was defeated at Plataea in 479 BC.
27731.m: After Salamis, the war turned in favour of the Greeks.

27732.q: In which city was Pericles the leading politician?
27732.e: Pericles shaped the politics of Athens from about 450 until his death in 429 BC. He came from a noble family.
27732.m: Pericles was the leading statesman of Athens.

27733.q: To which office was Pericles elected again and again for years?
27733.e: Generals were elected army leaders and had great political influence. From 443 BC, Pericles was re-elected almost every year.
27733.m: Pericles led Athens as an elected general.

27734.q: Which form of government did Pericles develop further in Athens?
27734.e: Under Pericles, all male citizens of Athens could have their say in the people’s assembly. Women, foreigners and slaves, however, were excluded.

27735.q: What did Pericles introduce so that poor citizens could also work as judges?
a: The right to vote for women
27735.e: Jurors received a small daily allowance for their work in the courts. This meant poor citizens could also afford to take part.
27735.m: Thanks to a daily allowance, poor Athenians could also take on political duties.

27736.q: What is the golden age of Athens around the middle of the 5th century BC called?
27736.e: In this period Athens flourished in art, theatre, philosophy and architecture. The name recalls the leading politician of the time.
27736.m: The Age of Pericles was the golden age of Athens.

27737.q: What was Pericles especially well known for among the Athenians?
27737.e: Pericles was a gifted speaker. With his speeches in the people’s assembly he convinced the Athenians of his plans again and again.

27738.q: What did Pericles die of in 429 BC?
27738.e: From 430 BC a terrible plague raged in the overcrowded city of Athens. Pericles also fell ill and died of it.
27738.m: Pericles died of the plague of Athens.

27739.q: With what did Pericles largely pay for his splendid buildings in Athens?
a: With money from the league of allies
27739.e: Athens’ allies paid contributions into a shared fund. Pericles used part of it for buildings in Athens, which was criticised.
27739.m: Pericles used the league’s money for the buildings of Athens.

27740.q: Which two powers mainly fought against each other in the Peloponnesian War?
27740.e: The two leading Greek cities fought for control of Greece. Both had many allies.
27740.m: In the Peloponnesian War, Athens fought against Sparta.

27741.q: Roughly how long did the Peloponnesian War last?
27741.e: The war began in 431 BC and ended in 404 BC with the defeat of Athens. So it lasted 27 years.
27741.m: The Peloponnesian War lasted almost 30 years.

27742.e: In 404 BC Athens had to surrender, pull down its Long Walls and give up its fleet. Sparta became the leading power in Greece.

27743.q: What is special about the history of the Peloponnesian War written by Thucydides?
a: He lived through the war himself
He wrote it as a poem
27743.e: Thucydides was himself an Athenian general. He looked for the causes of the war in people and not in the gods.
27743.m: Thucydides lived through the war he described.

27744.q: What was Athens especially strong in during the Peloponnesian War?
27744.e: Athens led a league of many islands and coastal cities. Sparta, on the other hand, was stronger on land.

27745.q: Which Athenian campaign ended in a terrible disaster in 413 BC?
27745.e: Athens wanted to conquer the city of Syracuse, but its army and fleet were almost completely destroyed. It never fully recovered.
27745.m: The Sicilian Expedition was Athens’ greatest defeat.

27746.q: Which foreign power supported Sparta towards the end of the war with money for a fleet?
27746.e: With Persian gold, Sparta was able to build a strong fleet. This let it defeat Athens at sea too.
27746.m: Persian money helped Sparta to win the war.

27747.q: What did Athens lose to Sparta at Aegospotami in 405 BC?
27747.e: The Spartan Lysander took the Athenians by surprise while their ships were on the beach. After that, Athens was cut off from grain.
27747.m: At Aegospotami, Athens lost its fleet.

27748.q: What is the Acropolis of Athens?
a: A large market square at the harbour
A royal palace in the valley
27748.e: Acropolis means “upper city”. On the rock above Athens stood temples for the city’s goddess Athena.
27748.m: The Acropolis is a fortified hill with temples above Athens.

27749.q: Which small temple on the Acropolis is dedicated to the goddess of victory?
27749.e: Nike is the Greek goddess of victory. Her small Ionic temple stands on a ledge next to the entrance.
27749.m: The Temple of Athena Nike honours Nike, goddess of victory.

27751.q: What is the best-known temple on the Acropolis of Athens called?
27751.e: The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC. The Pantheon, on the other hand, is in Rome.
27751.m: The Parthenon is the most famous temple on the Acropolis.

27752.q: What did the temples and statues on the Acropolis often look like originally?
27752.e: Today the marble buildings look white. But researchers have found traces of paint: many figures and decorations were once brightly painted.
27752.m: Greek temples and statues were often brightly painted in the past.

27753.q: What was the Parthenon used for in the Middle Ages?
27753.e: From about the 6th century AD the Parthenon served as a church. Later, under the Ottomans, it became a mosque.
27753.m: For a long time the Parthenon was a church.

27754.q: What destroyed large parts of the Parthenon in 1687?
a: The explosion of a gunpowder store
27754.e: The Ottomans stored gunpowder in the temple. During an attack by the Venetians, a cannonball hit the store and the building exploded.
27754.m: Since 1687 the Parthenon has been a ruin.

27755.q: What was performed in the ancient theatre on the slope of the Acropolis?
27755.e: On the south slope of the Acropolis, actors performed tragedies and comedies. The theatre of Athens is seen as the birthplace of European theatre.
27755.m: Tragedy and comedy began in ancient Athens.

27756.q: According to legend, which dragon-like monster was killed at Delphi?
27756.e: According to legend, the god of the sanctuary defeated the serpent Python. The name of the priestess, the Pythia, still recalls this.
27756.m: The legend of the dragon Python belongs to Delphi.

27757.q: What were the small buildings called in which Greek cities kept their offerings at Delphi?
27757.e: Many cities built their own treasury along the Sacred Way. The Treasury of the Athenians has been rebuilt.
27757.m: Precious offerings were kept in the treasuries of Delphi.

27758.q: Which famous bronze statue was found at Delphi in 1896?
27758.e: The Charioteer of Delphi dates from around 470 BC. It commemorates a victory in a chariot race.
27758.m: The Charioteer is one of the finest bronze statues in Greece.

27759.q: Why did the Oracle of Delphi come to an end after more than a thousand years?
a: A Christian emperor banned the old cults
27759.e: At the end of the 4th century, Emperor Theodosius I banned the old pagan cults. This also ended the oracle.
27759.m: The oracle ended when the old cults were banned.

27760.q: Which games were held at Delphi in honour of Apollo?
27760.e: The Pythian Games took place every four years. Besides sport, there were also contests in music and poetry.
27760.m: The Pythian Games took place at Delphi.

27761.q: According to Herodotus, what advice did the Oracle of Delphi give the Athenians before the great Persian attack?
a: To surround the city with stone walls
27761.e: The Athenians argued about what the saying meant. In the end they took the wooden walls to mean their ships.
27761.m: The Athenians took the “wooden walls” to mean their fleet.

27762.q: According to Herodotus, which rich king misunderstood the prophecy that he would destroy a great empire?
27762.e: The king of Lydia attacked the Persians and in doing so destroyed his own empire. The prophecy had had two meanings.
27762.m: Oracle sayings often had two meanings.

27763.q: What had to be moved for the great excavation of Delphi from 1892?
27763.e: A village lay on top of the ruins. It was moved to a new place so that French archaeologists could dig.
27763.m: A whole village moved for the excavation of Delphi.

27764.q: Which modern French city was founded by Greeks around 600 BC as Massalia?
27764.e: Settlers from Phocaea in Asia Minor founded Massalia. The city became an important trading place in the western Mediterranean.

27765.q: Which modern city in Italy was called Neapolis in Greek, meaning “new city”?
27765.e: Greeks from Cumae founded Neapolis in the 6th century BC next to the older settlement of Parthenope. The Italian name Napoli comes from it.

27766.q: On which seas did the Greeks found most of their colonies?
a: On the Mediterranean and the Black Sea
On the North Sea and the Baltic
On the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf
On the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean
27766.e: Greek settlers founded cities all around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, for example in Italy, France, Libya and on the coast of today’s Turkey.
27766.m: Greek colonies lay around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.

27767.q: What were southern Italy and Sicily called because of their many Greek cities?
27767.e: In Latin the area was called Magna Graecia. Cities such as Taras, Croton and Syracuse lay there.
27767.m: In ancient times, southern Italy was Greater Greece.

27768.q: What was an important reason for founding Greek colonies from the 8th century BC?
a: An order from the Persian king
27768.e: The population was growing, but there was little fertile land in Greece. Trade and political quarrels also played a part.
27768.m: A shortage of land drove many Greeks to emigrate.

27769.q: On which island did Greeks found the rich city of Syracuse?
27769.e: Syracuse lies on the east coast of Sicily. Greek settlers founded the city in the 8th century BC. It became one of the richest cities of the Greek world.
27769.m: Syracuse is a Greek foundation on Sicily.

27770.q: What did the Greeks call the city from which a colony was founded?
27770.e: Metropolis means “mother city”. The colony often stayed linked to it through religion and trade, but was politically independent.
27770.m: The mother city of a colony was called its metropolis.

27771.q: Whose conquests began the Hellenistic period?
27771.e: The Macedonian king conquered the Persian Empire as far as India. As a result, Greek culture spread throughout the East.
27771.m: The Hellenistic period began with Alexander the Great.

27772.q: How far east did Alexander the Great get with his conquests?
27772.e: Alexander conquered the whole Persian Empire and marched as far as the Indus in today’s Pakistan and India. There his soldiers refused to go any further.
27772.m: Alexander the Great got as far as India.

27773.q: What happened to Alexander the Great’s huge empire after his death?
a: It broke up into several kingdoms
It stayed united for hundreds of years
27773.e: Alexander’s generals fought over his empire and divided it among themselves. This created, for example, the kingdom of the Ptolemies in Egypt and that of the Seleucids in western Asia.
27773.m: Alexander’s empire broke up after his death.

27775.q: Which city in Egypt bears the name of Alexander the Great?
27775.e: Alexander founded Alexandria on the Mediterranean coast in 331 BC. In the Hellenistic period the city became a centre of Greek culture and science.
27775.m: Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great.

27776.q: Which language spread from Egypt to Persia in the Hellenistic period?
27776.e: After Alexander’s conquests, traders, officials and scholars all over the East spoke Greek. This common language is called Koine.
27776.m: In the Hellenistic period, Greek was the common language.

27777.q: With the death of which ruler did the last great Hellenistic kingdom end in 30 BC?
27777.e: Cleopatra was the last queen of the Ptolemaic dynasty. After her death, Egypt became a Roman province.
27777.m: The Hellenistic period ended with Cleopatra.

27778.q: Which philosopher was Plato a student of?
27778.e: Plato was a student of Socrates for many years. Socrates leads the conversation in almost all of Plato’s dialogues.

27779.q: What was the name of the school Plato founded in Athens around 387 BC?
27779.e: Plato founded his school in a grove dedicated to the hero Akademos. That is where the name Academy comes from, which is still used for colleges today.
27779.m: The word academy goes back to Plato’s school.

27780.q: In what form did Plato write most of his works?
27780.e: Plato wrote dialogues, that is conversations between several people. In this way he showed how you can reach knowledge through questions and answers.

27781.q: How did the trial of Plato’s teacher Socrates end?
a: He only had to pay a small fine
27781.e: In 399 BC Socrates was accused of corrupting the young. The court sentenced him to death, and he drank a cup of poison.

27782.q: What is the name of Plato’s famous work about the just state?
27782.e: “The Republic” (in Greek “Politeia”) describes how a just state should be organised. It is one of the most important books of political philosophy.
27782.m: In “The Republic”, Plato designs an ideal state.

27783.q: According to Plato, who should rule the ideal state?
27783.e: Plato believed that only those who know the truth and the good can rule justly. Therefore philosophers should rule, or rulers should become philosophers.

27784.q: What is Plato’s teaching called that behind visible things there are eternal, perfect original forms?
27784.e: According to the Theory of Forms, the things of the world are only imperfect copies of eternal Forms. A drawn circle, for example, is never as perfect as the Form of the circle.
27784.m: Plato’s Theory of Forms distinguishes copies from eternal original forms.

27785.q: According to Aristotle, which virtue is the right middle between cowardice and recklessness?
27785.e: Aristotle taught that a virtue is usually the middle between two bad extremes. Someone who is brave is neither cowardly nor reckless.
27785.m: For Aristotle, virtue lies in the right middle.

27786.q: How did Aristotle describe human beings in his work on the state?
a: As beings who live in a community
27786.e: Aristotle called the human being a “zoon politikon”, a living being that wants to live in a community. Only in the polis, he said, could people lead a good life.
27786.m: For Aristotle, humans are community beings.

27787.q: According to tradition, what did Aristotle like to do while teaching?
a: He stayed silent the whole time
27787.e: Aristotle is said to have walked up and down in a covered walkway while teaching. That is why his students were called the “Peripatetics”, those who walk about.
27787.m: Aristotle is said to have liked walking about while teaching.

27788.q: Roughly when did the philosopher Aristotle live?
27788.e: Aristotle was born in 384 BC and died in 322 BC. That is about 2400 years ago.

27789.q: Aristotle is seen as the founder of which study of correct reasoning?
27789.e: Aristotle was the first to study systematically when a conclusion is valid. A well-known example is the syllogism with two premises and a conclusion.
27789.m: Aristotle is seen as the father of logic.

27790.q: According to Aristotle, which four elements made up the world on Earth?
27790.e: The Greeks thought that everything on Earth was a mixture of earth, water, air and fire. For the heavens, Aristotle assumed a fifth element as well.
27790.m: The four elements of the Greeks are earth, water, air and fire.

27791.q: In Aristotle’s view of the world, what was at the centre of the universe?
27791.e: Aristotle held a geocentric view of the world, in which the Sun, the Moon and the stars move around the Earth, which stays still. This view was accepted in Europe for almost 2000 years.
27791.m: Aristotle put the Earth at the centre of the universe.

27792.q: Aristotle described and classified hundreds of kinds of animals. Which subject is he therefore seen as the founder of?
27792.e: Aristotle observed animals closely, dissected them and sorted them into groups. In this way he laid the foundation for the scientific study of animals.
27792.m: Aristotle is seen as the founder of zoology.

27793.q: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is 13 cm long and one of the shorter sides is 5 cm. How long is the other shorter side?
27793.e: 13² minus 5² = 169 minus 25 = 144. The square root of 144 is 12, so the other side is 12 cm long.
27793.m: Pythagoras’ theorem also helps you find a missing shorter side.

27794.q: What is Pythagoras’ theorem, with the shorter sides a and b and the hypotenuse c?
27794.e: The squares on the two shorter sides together have the same area as the square on the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse lies opposite the right angle.
27794.m: The squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the hypotenuse.

27795.q: A right-angled triangle has two shorter sides of 3 cm and 4 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
27795.e: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25. The square root of 25 is 5, so the hypotenuse is 5 cm long.
27795.m: The triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 is a well-known right-angled triangle.

27796.q: What did Pythagoras and his followers believe about the soul?
a: It lives in the head of a god
It only comes into being in old age
27796.e: Pythagoras taught the transmigration of souls: after death the soul passes into a new body, even that of an animal. That is why animals should be respected.
27796.m: Pythagoras believed in the transmigration of the soul.

27797.q: What are the followers of Pythagoras called?
27797.e: The followers of Pythagoras were called Pythagoreans. They lived together in a community with strict rules and studied numbers and music.
27797.m: The students of Pythagoras were called Pythagoreans.

27798.q: For the Pythagoreans, what was the origin and order of all things?
27798.e: The Pythagoreans believed that the whole world could be explained with numbers and ratios. They saw number as the essence of all things.
27798.m: For the Pythagoreans, everything was number.

27799.q: The Pythagoreans studied the notes made by strings. Which interval sounds when you halve a string exactly?
27799.e: The half string vibrates twice as fast and sounds an octave higher. The ratio 2 to 1 showed the Pythagoreans that music is based on numbers.
27799.m: A halved string sounds an octave higher.

27800.q: What is Archimedes said to have shouted when he had an idea in the bath?
27800.e: “Eureka” is Greek and means “I have found it!”. Archimedes is said to have been so excited that he jumped straight out of the bath.

27801.q: On which island did the Greek scientist Archimedes live?
27801.e: Archimedes lived in Syracuse on Sicily. At that time it was a rich Greek city.

27802.q: According to Archimedes’ principle, how big is the upward force on an object in water?
a: As big as the weight of the water pushed aside
As big as the weight of the object itself
Twice as big as the weight of the object
Always exactly the same as in air
27802.e: An object pushes water aside and is pushed upwards by a force equal to the weight of that water. That is why a ship floats if it pushes aside enough water.
27802.m: The upward force equals the weight of the liquid pushed aside.

27803.q: What did Archimedes use his machines for when the Romans attacked his city?
27803.e: Archimedes built cranes and catapults against the Roman ships. In this way the city held out against the siege for a long time.
27803.m: Archimedes defended his city with machines.

27804.q: “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the world.” Which tool did Archimedes mean?
27804.e: Archimedes described the law of the lever: with a long lever you can move a heavy load with little force. The saying shows how powerful this principle is.
27804.m: With a long lever you can move heavy loads.

27805.q: Which army conquered Archimedes’ home city in 212 BC, killing him?
27805.e: In the Second Punic War, the Romans besieged and conquered the city. A Roman soldier is said to have killed Archimedes, even though the general wanted to spare him.
27805.m: Archimedes died in 212 BC during a Roman conquest.

27806.q: Which number did Archimedes estimate amazingly accurately with the help of polygons?
27806.e: Archimedes drew polygons with up to 96 sides inside and outside a circle. In this way he found that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7.
27806.m: Archimedes narrowed down pi using polygons.

27807.q: What is Euclid’s famous main work called?
27807.e: In the “Elements”, Euclid brought together the mathematical knowledge of his time in an orderly way. The work was used as a textbook for over 2000 years.
27807.m: Euclid’s “Elements” is one of the most influential textbooks in history.

27808.q: What was Euclid’s “Elements” used for over 2000 years?
27808.e: In the “Elements”, Euclid brought together the mathematical knowledge of his time in 13 books. Pupils learned from it until the 19th century.
27808.m: Euclid’s “Elements” was for a long time the most important maths book.

27809.q: Euclid is often called the “father” of which area of mathematics?
27809.e: Euclid built up the study of points, lines, angles and shapes in a strictly logical way. That is why we still speak of “Euclidean geometry” today.
27809.m: Euclid is seen as the father of geometry.

27810.q: In which city did Euclid teach around 300 BC?
27810.e: Euclid worked in Alexandria in Egypt, which was a centre of science at the time. Otherwise very little is known about his life.

27811.q: What did Euclid prove about prime numbers?
27811.e: Euclid showed that if there were only finitely many prime numbers, their product plus 1 would lead to a contradiction. So there are infinitely many.
27811.m: According to Euclid, there are infinitely many prime numbers.

27812.q: What do you work out with the Euclidean algorithm?
a: The square root of a number
27812.e: In the Euclidean algorithm you keep dividing with remainders until the remainder is zero. The last divisor is the highest common factor of two numbers.
27812.m: The Euclidean algorithm finds the highest common factor.

27813.q: Which famous postulate of Euclid is about straight lines that never meet?
27813.e: Put simply, the parallel postulate says that through a point outside a line there is exactly one parallel line. Mathematicians discussed it for centuries.
27813.m: The parallel postulate is about lines that never meet.

27814.q: What did Hippocratic doctors often begin a treatment with?
27814.e: Hippocratic medicine put great value on diet, meaning healthy food, exercise and rest. Only if that did not help did doctors turn to medicines or operations.
27814.m: Hippocratic doctors relied first on a healthy way of life.

27815.q: Which principle for doctors comes from the Hippocratic writings?
a: Help, or at least do no harm
27815.e: The writings say that a doctor should help the sick or at least not harm them. This principle still applies in medicine today.
27815.m: Above all, a doctor should do no harm.

27816.q: How many bodily fluids, or humours, did the Hippocratic theory of humours distinguish?
27816.e: Illness was seen as a disturbance in the balance of these humours. The theory of humours shaped medicine in Europe until modern times.
27816.m: The ancient theory of humours knew four bodily fluids.

27817.q: What did Hippocrates and his students teach about the causes of illnesses?
a: They are punishments from the gods
27817.e: Hippocratic doctors looked for the causes of illness in diet, way of life, climate and surroundings. They rejected punishment by the gods as an explanation.
27817.m: Hippocrates explained illnesses with natural causes.

a: An oath taken by athletes at Olympia
27818.e: The oath goes back to the school of Hippocrates. In it, doctors promised to help the sick and not to harm them.
27818.m: The Hippocratic Oath is a promise made by doctors.

27819.q: What did Hippocratic doctors pay particular attention to when treating patients?
27819.e: The doctors examined the sick carefully and wrote down how the illness developed. In this way they could make predictions and pass on their experience.
27819.m: Hippocratic doctors observed their patients closely.

27820.q: What is Hippocrates still seen as today?
a: The inventor of the Olympic Games
27820.e: Hippocrates lived on the island of Kos and founded a famous school of medicine. He explained illnesses with natural causes.
27820.m: Hippocrates is seen as the father of medicine.

27821.q: Which of these fluids was part of the theory of humours in ancient medicine?
27821.e: Black bile was one of the bodily fluids in the theory of humours. The Greek word melancholy literally means “black bile”.
27821.m: The word melancholy comes from black bile.

27822.q: The Roman Cicero called the Greek Herodotus the “father” of which subject?
27822.e: Cicero called Herodotus “pater historiae”, the father of history. Herodotus wanted to record what people had done so that it would not be forgotten.
27822.m: Herodotus is seen as the father of history.

27823.q: What is Herodotus’ great work called?
27823.e: Herodotus’ work is called the “Histories”, which means roughly “inquiries”. It was later divided into nine books.

27824.q: Which war is at the centre of Herodotus’ work?
27824.e: Herodotus describes the fighting between the Greeks and the Persian Empire in the 5th century BC. This includes battles such as Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis.
27824.m: Herodotus tells the story of the Persian Wars.

27825.q: In which modern country is Herodotus’ birthplace, today’s Bodrum?
27825.e: Herodotus came from Halicarnassus on the coast of Asia Minor. Today the place is called Bodrum and lies in Turkey.
27825.m: Herodotus came from the area of today’s Turkey.

27826.q: Which country did Herodotus call a “gift of the river”?
27826.e: Herodotus thought that Egypt owed its fertility to the Nile. Every year, the river’s flood brought fertile mud.
27826.m: For Herodotus, Egypt was a gift of the Nile.

27827.q: In which century did Herodotus live?
27827.e: Herodotus lived from about 484 to 425 BC. So he wrote only a few decades after the events he described.
27827.m: Herodotus lived in the 5th century BC.

27828.q: Where did Herodotus get a lot of the information for his work?
27828.e: Herodotus travelled to Egypt and to the Black Sea, among other places. He asked people questions and wrote down what they told him, even if he did not believe everything.
27828.m: Herodotus gathered his knowledge on his travels.

27829.q: According to Thales, what was the original substance from which everything came?
27829.e: Thales thought that everything had come from water. He was one of the first to look for a natural rather than a mythical explanation of the world.
27829.m: For Thales, water was the origin of all things.

27830.q: Which event in the sky is Thales said to have predicted for the year 585 BC?
27830.e: According to Herodotus, Thales predicted a solar eclipse. It took place on 28 May 585 BC during a battle, after which the enemies made peace.
27830.m: Thales is said to have predicted the solar eclipse of 585 BC.

27831.q: One side of a triangle is the diameter of a circle and the third corner lies on the circle. How big is the angle at this corner?
27831.e: This is Thales’ theorem: every angle in a semicircle measures 90 degrees. It is true wherever the corner lies on the arc.
27831.m: Every angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

27832.q: How is Thales said to have worked out the height of the Egyptian pyramids?
a: With a rope from the top
By counting the rows of stones
With the weight of the stones
27832.e: Thales is said to have waited until his own shadow was as long as he was tall. At that moment the pyramid’s shadow was also as long as its height.
27832.m: Thales measured heights with the help of shadows.

27833.q: Which famous group did the ancient Greeks count Thales among?
27833.e: The Seven Sages were famous thinkers and statesmen of early Greek times. Thales is named in all the lists that have come down to us.
27833.m: Thales was one of the Seven Sages of Greece.

27834.q: Which material is Thales said to have studied that attracts light things after being rubbed?
27834.e: When rubbed, amber attracts hairs or feathers. The Greek word for amber, “elektron”, is found today in the word electricity.
27834.m: The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber.

27835.q: Which measurement did Eratosthenes work out amazingly accurately around 240 BC?
27835.e: Eratosthenes compared the position of the Sun at two places in Egypt. From this he calculated the Earth’s circumference with a very small error for that time.
27835.m: Eratosthenes was the first to calculate the Earth’s circumference.

27836.q: What did Eratosthenes observe on the longest day of the year in a town in the south of Egypt?
a: At midday the Sun shone right to the bottom of the wells
The Sun did not rise at all
It snowed for the first time
27836.e: In Syene, today’s Aswan, the Sun was almost directly overhead at midday. That is why wells cast no shadow.
27836.m: At the summer solstice the Sun was almost directly overhead in Syene.

27837.q: What job did Eratosthenes have in Alexandria?
a: He was the king’s personal doctor
27837.e: Eratosthenes was brought to Alexandria by the Egyptian king and ran the famous library there. This gave him access to many writings and measurements.
27837.m: Eratosthenes was head of the Library of Alexandria.

27838.q: Two places are 5000 stadia apart. This distance is one fiftieth of the Earth’s circumference. What circumference does that give?
27838.e: You calculate 5000 times 50 = 250,000 stadia. Depending on how long a stadion was, that is about 39,000 to 46,000 kilometres.
27838.m: Eratosthenes multiplied the distance by 50 and got the Earth’s circumference.

27839.q: Roughly how big is the Earth’s circumference at the equator according to modern measurements?
27839.e: The Earth’s circumference at the equator is about 40,075 kilometres. Eratosthenes’ figure was amazingly close to it.
27839.m: The Earth has a circumference of about 40,000 kilometres.

27840.q: Which numbers do you find with the “Sieve of Eratosthenes”?
27840.e: You write down all the numbers and cross out the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and so on, one after another. What is left are the prime numbers.
27840.m: The Sieve of Eratosthenes sifts out the prime numbers.

27841.q: What did Eratosthenes assume about the Sun’s rays in his calculation?
a: They reach the Earth in parallel
They are bent by the Moon
They are shorter in the south
27841.e: Because the Sun is very far away, its rays arrive almost parallel. The different shadow angles at two places then show the curve of the Earth.
27841.m: Parallel sunrays made it possible to measure the Earth’s curve.

27842.q: Eratosthenes is also seen as the founder of which science?
27842.e: Eratosthenes wrote a work describing the Earth and drew a map of the world with lines on it. He is seen as the founder of scientific geography.
27842.m: Eratosthenes is seen as the founder of geography.

27843.q: What did Democritus call the smallest particles that everything is made of?
27843.e: Democritus taught that all things are made of tiny, invisible particles. He called them atoms, a term physics still uses today.
27843.m: Democritus called the smallest particles atoms.

27844.q: What does the Greek word “atomos” mean?
27844.e: “Atomos” means “that which cannot be divided”. Democritus thought you could not divide substances endlessly; at some point you would reach a particle that cannot be divided any further.
27844.m: Atom means that which cannot be divided.

27845.e: Democritus thought atoms were so small that they could not be seen. They differ only in shape, size and position.
27845.m: According to Democritus, atoms are tiny and invisible.

27846.q: According to Democritus, what is there between the atoms?
27846.e: For Democritus there were only atoms and the void. In empty space the atoms can move and rearrange themselves.
27846.m: According to Democritus, there are only atoms and empty space.

27847.q: Which nickname did Democritus get because of his cheerful nature?
27847.e: Democritus is said to have laughed at people’s foolishness and taught that cheerfulness is a great good. The weeping philosopher, on the other hand, was Heraclitus.

27848.q: Which country did the philosopher Democritus come from?
27848.e: Democritus was born around 460 BC in Abdera, a Greek city on the northern coast of the Aegean.

27849.q: According to Democritus, what happens when a thing comes into being or passes away?
