27849.e: The atoms themselves are eternal and unchanging. Things come into being when atoms gather together and pass away when they separate again.
27849.m: For Democritus, every change is just atoms rearranging themselves.

27850.e: Lambda is written Λ or λ and pronounced like L. In physics, λ often stands for wavelength.
27850.m: The Greek lambda matches the L.

27851.q: Which Greek letter looks like our P but is pronounced like “R”?
27851.e: Capital rho is written as P, but it is an R sound. That is why Greek words are easy to misread.
27851.m: The Greek P is called rho and sounds like R.

27852.q: How did the lines run in an early Greek way of writing called “as the ox ploughs”?
a: Alternately to the right and to the left
In a circle around the middle
27852.e: An ox turns at the end of each furrow and ploughs back. In the same way, the direction changed with every line in this way of writing. Later, writing from left to right became the rule.
27852.m: In “ox-plough” writing, the direction changed with every line.

27853.q: What important new feature did the Greeks add to the script they took over?
27853.e: The Phoenician script only had signs for consonants. The Greeks used some signs in a new way for vowels such as A, E and O.
27853.m: The Greeks were the first to write vowels too.

27854.q: Which Greek capital letter is shaped like a triangle?
27854.e: Capital delta is written as a triangle. That is why triangular river mouths, such as that of the Nile, are also called a delta.
27854.m: Capital delta looks like a triangle.

27855.q: Which modern script, used for example in Russia, developed from the Greek alphabet?
27855.e: The Cyrillic script was created in the 9th and 10th centuries, mainly based on the Greek capital letters. Today it is used in Russia, Bulgaria, Serbia and other countries.
27855.m: The Cyrillic script comes from the Greek alphabet.

27856.q: Which Greek letter is used in maths as the sign for a sum?
27856.e: Capital sigma Σ matches our S as in “sum”. Mathematicians use it as a short way to show that many numbers are added together.
27856.m: In maths, capital sigma stands for a sum.

27857.q: In honour of which god were the great theatre festivals held in Athens?
27857.e: The plays were performed at the Dionysia, festivals for Dionysus, the god of wine and fertility. The theatre in Athens lay in his sacred area.
27857.m: Greek theatre began at festivals for Dionysus.

27858.q: What is the serious kind of play called in which the main character often falls into misfortune?
27858.e: In a tragedy, a hero gets into a serious conflict that he cannot solve. The audience were meant to feel pity and fear.
27858.m: Tragedy is the serious drama of the Greeks.

27859.q: What were the rising rows of seats in a Greek theatre called, whose name means “place for watching”?
27859.e: The theatron was the seating area for the audience, usually built into a hillside. Our word theatre comes from this word.
27859.m: The word theatre comes from the Greek theatron.

27860.q: What was the stage building behind the acting area called, from which our word “scene” comes?
27860.e: At first the skene was a simple tent or hut in which the actors changed their costumes. Later it was developed into a stage wall with doors.
27860.m: The word scene comes from the Greek skene.

27861.q: Who was allowed to act on stage in ancient Athens?
27861.e: All roles, even women’s roles, were played by men. With masks and costumes they played the different characters.
27861.m: In Greek theatre only men acted.

27862.q: Which ancient theatre in Greece is famous for its excellent acoustics?
27862.e: In the theatre of Epidaurus you can hear even a quiet sound from the stage in the very top rows. It had room for about 14,000 spectators and is still used for performances today.
27862.m: The theatre of Epidaurus has famous acoustics.

27867.q: Which order of columns do the columns in the porch of the Pantheon in Rome show?
27867.e: The 16 columns of the Pantheon’s porch have capitals decorated with acanthus leaves. The Romans preferred the splendid Corinthian style.
27867.m: The Pantheon in Rome has Corinthian columns.

27868.q: What do many Greek columns have on their shaft?
27868.e: The vertical grooves are called flutes. They make the column look slimmer and create a play of light and shadow.
27868.m: Greek columns often have vertical grooves called flutes.

27869.q: On the Erechtheion in Athens, what holds up the roof of a porch instead of columns?
27869.e: On the Erechtheion on the Acropolis, six female figures hold up the roof. Such supporting figures are called caryatids.
27869.m: Caryatids are female figures that serve as columns.

27870.q: The Ionic order is named after the region of Ionia. Where was Ionia?
a: On the coast of Asia Minor
27870.e: Ionia was an area with Greek cities on the west coast of Asia Minor. The Ionic style of building developed there in the 6th century BC.
27870.m: The Ionic order comes from Ionia in Asia Minor.

27871.q: What was mainly collected in the Library of Alexandria?
27871.e: The library collected scrolls from many countries. Books in the form we know today did not yet exist.
27871.m: The Library of Alexandria held scrolls.

27872.q: What were the “Pinakes” in the Library of Alexandria used for?
a: As a catalogue of the books
27872.e: In the “Pinakes”, the poet Callimachus sorted authors and works by subject. They are seen as one of the first library catalogues.
27872.m: The Pinakes were an early library catalogue.

27873.q: From which city is an Egyptian king said to have borrowed the original texts of the great tragedies and never given them back?
27873.e: The king left a large deposit in silver but kept the originals and sent back only copies. The deposit was lost, but the library had the valuable texts.
27873.m: Alexandria kept Athens’ originals of the tragedies.

27874.q: According to ancient reports, how many scrolls is the library said to have owned?
27874.e: Ancient sources give figures of about 400,000 to 700,000 scrolls. The exact number is uncertain, but it was the largest library of the ancient world.
27874.m: The Library of Alexandria probably owned hundreds of thousands of scrolls.

27875.q: Into which language was the Hebrew Bible translated in Alexandria?
27875.e: Many people in Alexandria spoke Greek. The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible is called the Septuagint.
27875.m: The Hebrew Bible was translated into Greek in Alexandria.

27876.q: To which research centre, dedicated to the Muses, did the Library of Alexandria belong?
27876.e: The Mouseion was a place where scholars did research, taught and ate together. Our word museum comes from the word Mouseion.
27876.m: The library belonged to the Mouseion of Alexandria.

27877.q: Which Roman general fought in Alexandria in 48 BC, when a fire is said to have destroyed many books?
27877.e: In the Alexandrian War, Caesar had ships in the harbour set on fire. The fire is said to have spread to warehouses with books; how many is disputed.
27877.m: During Caesar’s fighting in Alexandria, many books probably burned.

27878.q: What important task did the consuls have in war?
27878.e: The consuls held the “imperium”, the highest power of command. In war they led the Roman legions as generals.
27878.m: In war, the consuls were Rome’s highest commanders.

27879.q: Who usually belonged to the Senate in the Roman Republic?
27879.e: The Senate was mostly made up of men who had already held high offices. They advised the consuls with their experience.
27879.m: Experienced former office holders sat in the Senate.

27880.q: What does the Roman abbreviation SPQR stand for?
a: The Senate and People of Rome
State of the Provinces of Rome
27880.e: SPQR means “Senatus Populusque Romanus”, that is “the Senate and the People of Rome”. The abbreviation appeared on army standards, coins and buildings.
27880.m: SPQR means “the Senate and the People of Rome”.

27881.q: How long did a senator normally belong to the Senate in the Roman Republic?
27881.e: Senators usually stayed in the Senate for life, as long as they were not expelled for serious offences. Many of them were former office holders with a lot of experience.
27881.m: A Roman senator usually stayed in the Senate all his life.

27882.q: What did a consul’s attendants carry as a sign of his power?
27882.e: The attendants were called lictors. Their bundles of rods, the fasces, showed that the consul had the right to punish.
27882.m: Bundles of rods showed the power of the consul.

27883.q: How did the Romans name a year in the time of the Republic?
a: After the names of the two consuls
After the name of the king
27883.e: The Romans named a year after the two consuls who were in office that year. Being consul was therefore a great honour for the whole family.
27883.m: The Romans named each year after its consuls.

27884.q: Who ruled Rome before the time of the Republic?
27884.e: At first, Rome was ruled by kings. After the last king was driven out, Rome became a republic.
27884.m: Before the Republic, Rome was ruled by kings.

27885.q: How could you recognise a Roman senator by his clothes?
a: By a broad purple stripe on his tunic
By red boots with little bells
27885.e: Senators wore a tunic with a broad purple stripe, the “latus clavus”. Purple was very expensive and was a sign of high rank.
27885.m: A broad purple stripe showed that someone was a senator.

27886.q: What was the highest office in the Roman Republic?
27886.e: The two consuls stood at the head of the state. Anyone who wanted to become consul first had to hold lower offices.
27886.m: Consul was the highest office of the Republic.

27887.q: Who were the patricians in Rome?
27887.e: The patricians were a small group of old, noble families. At first only they held the high offices and positions as priests.
27887.m: The patricians were the old nobility of Rome.

27888.q: With which parable is Menenius Agrippa said to have persuaded the plebeians who had left the city to return?
27888.e: Menenius Agrippa compared the state to a body. The limbs harm themselves if they stop feeding the stomach, just as the parts of the people need one another.
27888.m: Menenius Agrippa compared Rome to a body whose parts need one another.

27889.q: What means of pressure did the plebeians use to get their demands in the Conflict of the Orders?
a: They all left the city together.
They set fire to the Senate.
They called on a foreign king for help.
27889.e: In a “secessio”, the plebeians left the city together. Without them, Rome lacked workers and above all soldiers, so the patricians had to give way.
27889.m: By leaving the city, the plebeians forced through more rights.

27890.q: What did a Roman law of 445 BC allow for the first time?
a: The right to vote for slaves
27890.e: Before that, patricians and plebeians were not allowed to marry each other. The law was called the Lex Canuleia, after the tribune Gaius Canuleius.
27890.m: From 445 BC, patricians and plebeians were allowed to marry.

27891.q: Which high office did the Licinian-Sextian laws open to the plebeians in 367 BC?
27891.e: Under these laws, one of the two consuls could be a plebeian. In 366 BC Lucius Sextius was elected as the first plebeian consul.
27891.m: From 367 BC, plebeians could also become consul.

27892.q: How did the Conflict of the Orders in Rome end?
a: The plebeians got almost the same rights as the patricians
27892.e: After about 200 years of struggle, the Lex Hortensia of 287 BC made the decisions of the plebeians binding on all Romans. With this, the plebeians were largely equal.
27892.m: At the end of the Conflict of the Orders, the plebeians had almost equal rights.

27893.q: What was a noble protector in Rome who supported his clients called?
27893.e: A patron helped his clients, for example in court or with money. In return, the clients supported him in elections and went with him in public.
27893.m: Patron and client were linked by duties to each other.

27894.q: In the early Republic, what harsh consequence did poor plebeians face if they could not pay back their debts?
27894.e: Anyone who could not pay their debts had to work for the lender and practically lost their freedom. This debt bondage was an important reason for the Conflict of the Orders.
27894.m: Fear of debt bondage drove the plebeians to resist.

27895.q: Why did the Roman emperors have the power of a tribune of the people given to them?
a: So that they could not be harmed and could stop decisions
So that they could run gladiator fights
So that they did not have to pay taxes
So that they became priests of Vesta
27895.e: The emperors held the “tribunicia potestas”, the power of a tribune of the people. This made them untouchable and allowed them to block any decision.
27895.m: The emperors used the powers of the tribunes for their own power.

27896.q: What does the Latin word “veto”, with which a tribune of the people could stop decisions, mean?
27896.e: By calling out “veto”, a tribune of the people could block decisions made by officials and by the Senate. We still use the word veto today.

27897.q: What special protection did a tribune of the people enjoy during his time in office?
a: He was allowed to carry weapons in the Senate.
He did not have to pay taxes.
27897.e: Tribunes of the people were seen as “sacrosanctus”, that is sacred and untouchable. Anyone who used violence against a tribune could be killed without punishment.
27897.m: A tribune of the people was untouchable and could not be attacked.

27898.q: How many tribunes of the people were later elected each year in the Roman Republic?
27898.e: At first there were only a few tribunes; from the middle of the 5th century BC, ten were elected every year. Each of them could use his veto on his own.
27898.m: Every year the plebeians elected ten tribunes of the people.

27899.q: Which assembly did the tribunes of the people lead?
a: The council of the Vestal Virgins
27899.e: The tribunes of the people called together the “Concilium plebis”, the assembly of the plebeians. Plebiscites were decided there.
27899.m: The tribunes of the people led the assembly of the plebeians.

27900.q: Who was not allowed to become a tribune of the people in the Roman Republic?
27900.e: Only plebeians could become tribunes of the people. The patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher even had himself adopted by a plebeian so that he could hold the office.
27900.m: Only plebeians could become tribunes of the people.

27901.q: What did a tribune of the people have to do with his front door so that people seeking help could reach him at any time?
a: Leave it open day and night
Paint it with his coat of arms
Only open it on market day
27901.e: A tribune’s door was meant to stand open day and night. This meant plebeians could always ask for help.
27901.m: A tribune’s door was always open to those seeking help.

27902.q: Around which year was the Law of the Twelve Tables written down in Rome?
27902.e: The Law of the Twelve Tables was created around 451 to 450 BC. It is seen as Rome’s oldest written law code.
27902.m: The Law of the Twelve Tables was created around 450 BC.

27903.q: Where were the tablets of the Law of the Twelve Tables put up in public?
27903.e: The tablets stood in the Roman Forum, the centre of public life. This meant every citizen could read the law.
27903.m: The Law of the Twelve Tables was visible to everyone in the Forum.

27904.q: According to tradition, who wrote down the Law of the Twelve Tables?
27904.e: A board of ten men, the decemvirs, was set up to write the laws down. During this time they ruled instead of the consuls.
27904.m: Ten men, the decemvirs, wrote down the Law of the Twelve Tables.

27905.q: Why was the Law of the Twelve Tables so important for the plebeians?
a: The law was now written down and anyone could read it.
27905.e: Before that, it was mainly patrician priests and judges who knew the rules of the law. Written law protected the plebeians better against unfair judgements.
27905.m: Written law protects against arbitrary decisions.

27906.q: According to tradition, which Greek city did Roman envoys visit to study its laws?
27906.e: According to Livy, envoys travelled to Athens to learn about the laws of Solon. Whether this journey really took place is disputed among historians.
27906.m: According to tradition, Athens served as a model for the Law of the Twelve Tables.

27907.q: According to Cicero, what did Roman children have to do with the Law of the Twelve Tables?
27907.e: Cicero reports that boys learned the Law of the Twelve Tables by heart like a set poem. This shows how important it was to the Romans.
27907.m: Roman pupils learned the Law of the Twelve Tables by heart.

27908.q: How were the original tablets of the Law of the Twelve Tables probably lost?
a: When the Gauls invaded Rome around 387 BC
27908.e: It is thought that the tablets were destroyed when the Gauls invaded around 387 BC. Their content is only known from quotations by later writers.
27908.m: We only know the content of the Law of the Twelve Tables from quotations.

27909.q: Who fought against each other in the Punic Wars?
27909.e: Rome and Carthage fought for more than 100 years over control of the western Mediterranean. In the end Rome won.
27909.m: In the Punic Wars, Rome fought Carthage.

27910.q: Where does the word “Punic” come from?
a: From the Latin name for the Phoenicians
From the name of a river in Africa
From the name of a Roman general
27910.e: The Romans called the Carthaginians “Poeni”, meaning Phoenicians. The word “Punic” comes from this.
27910.m: “Punic” comes from the Latin word for the Phoenicians.

27911.q: Which island did Rome and Carthage mainly fight over in the First Punic War?
27911.e: The First Punic War was about control of Sicily. After the victory, the island became the first Roman province.

27912.q: In the First Punic War, what did the Romans first have to build up in order to defeat Carthage?
27912.e: Carthage was a great sea power. So the Romans built many warships in a short time and learned to fight at sea.
27912.m: In the First Punic War, Rome became a sea power.

27913.q: Which of the Punic Wars is also called the “Hannibalic War”?
27913.e: In the Second Punic War (218 to 201 BC), Hannibal led the Carthaginians. That is why it is also called the Hannibalic War.
27913.m: The Second Punic War is also called the Hannibalic War.

27914.q: Who won the First Punic War?
27914.e: After a victory at sea west of Sicily, Rome forced Carthage to make peace in 241 BC. Sicily became Roman.
27914.m: Rome won the First Punic War.

27915.q: How did the Romans at first fight against Hannibal to avoid big defeats?
a: They avoided big battles and only made small attacks
They built a wall across the Alps
27915.e: The general Fabius Maximus avoided open battles. With small attacks he weakened Hannibal’s army, which hardly got any supplies so far from home.
27915.m: Against Hannibal, the Romans at first avoided big battles.

27916.q: What did the Romans do to Carthage in 146 BC at the end of the Third Punic War?
27916.e: After a long siege, the Romans captured Carthage and destroyed it. The area became the Roman province of Africa.
27916.m: In 146 BC the Romans destroyed Carthage.

27917.q: After the peace of 201 BC, what was Carthage no longer allowed to do?
a: Go to war without Rome’s permission
27917.e: Carthage had to give up almost its entire fleet and was no longer allowed to wage war without Rome’s consent. When it defended itself against Numidia anyway, Rome used this as an excuse for a new war.
27917.m: After 201 BC, Carthage needed Rome’s permission for any war.

27918.q: Which city was Carthage’s great rival in ancient times?
27918.e: Rome and Carthage fought three Punic Wars for control of the western Mediterranean. In the end Rome won.
27918.m: Rome and Carthage were bitter rivals.

27919.e: Carthage was founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, a port city in today’s Lebanon. The Phoenicians were famous traders and sailors.
27919.m: Carthage was founded by the Phoenicians.

27922.q: What were the Carthaginians especially well known for?
27922.e: Carthage had a large fleet and traded all over the Mediterranean. Carthaginian sailors even explored the west coast of Africa.
27922.m: The Carthaginians were famous sailors and traders.

27923.q: What does Carthage’s Phoenician name, “Qart-Hadasht”, mean?
27923.e: Qart-Hadasht means “New City”. In Latin this name became “Carthago”.

27924.q: What can still be seen of the city of Carthage today?
a: Ruins from Punic and Roman times
27924.e: After the destruction in 146 BC, the Romans built a new city there. Today you can see ruins from both periods. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27924.m: In Carthage you can see Punic and Roman ruins.

27925.q: Which city did the general Hannibal come from?
27925.e: Hannibal was a general from Carthage in North Africa. His father had already fought against Rome.
27925.m: Hannibal was a general from Carthage.

27926.q: From which region did Hannibal set out on his campaign against Rome?
27926.e: Hannibal started in Spain, where Carthage had bases such as Carthago Nova (today Cartagena). From there he marched over the Pyrenees and the Alps to Italy.
27926.m: Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps to Italy.

27927.q: In which country did Hannibal fight the Romans for many years after crossing the Alps?
27927.e: After crossing the Alps, Hannibal marched through Italy and defeated the Romans several times. He stayed in Italy for about 15 years but could not conquer Rome.
27927.m: Hannibal fought against Rome in Italy for many years.

27928.q: Which animals did Hannibal take with him on his campaign over the Alps?
27928.e: According to ancient reports, Hannibal marched to Italy with 37 war elephants. Most of them did not survive the harsh winter and the fighting for long.
27928.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants.

27929.q: What made Hannibal’s route over the Alps especially dangerous?
a: High waves and storms at sea
27929.e: Hannibal crossed the Alps in autumn. Cold, snow, narrow paths and attacks by mountain peoples cost many soldiers and animals their lives.
27929.m: Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps was very dangerous because of cold and snow.

27930.q: What do we know today about the exact pass Hannibal used?
a: It is marked on a Roman map.
27930.e: Researchers suggest different passes, for example the Col de la Traversette, the Mont Cenis or the Little St Bernard. There is still no clear proof.
27930.m: Exactly which Alpine pass Hannibal took is still unclear.

27931.q: According to Livy, how did Hannibal’s soldiers break up a rock in their way?
a: They heated it with fire and poured vinegar over it.
They had elephants push it away.
They knocked it away with golden hammers.
27931.e: Livy tells how the rock was heated with fire and then doused with vinegar until it crumbled. Whether this is true is not certain.
27931.m: According to Livy, Hannibal broke up a rock with fire and vinegar.

27932.q: Who won the long war between Rome and Hannibal in the end?
27932.e: Hannibal won several times in Italy, but Rome did not give up. In 202 BC Hannibal was defeated in North Africa, and Carthage had to make peace.
27932.m: In the end Rome won the war against Hannibal.

27933.q: Who were the Gracchi in ancient Rome?
27933.e: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus were brothers from a noble family. As tribunes of the people, both tried to push through reforms.
27933.m: The Gracchi were two brothers who wanted to reform Rome.

27934.q: What did the Gracchi want to achieve for poor farmers in Rome?
a: That they get their own land
27934.e: Many farmers had lost their land, while rich people owned huge estates. The Gracchi wanted to share out state land among poor citizens.
27934.m: The Gracchi wanted to share out land among poor citizens.

27935.q: How were Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus related?
27935.e: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus were brothers. As politicians in Rome, both stood up for poor citizens. Together they are called the Gracchi.

27936.q: What did Tiberius Gracchus want to achieve with his land law?
a: Share out state land among poor citizens
27936.e: Many small farmers had lost their land, while the rich used large parts of the state land. Tiberius wanted to share out this land again among poor citizens.
27936.m: Tiberius Gracchus wanted to give land back to poor citizens.

27937.q: What did the land law of Tiberius Gracchus aim to limit?
a: How much state land one person could own
How many children a family could have
How many soldiers Rome could have
How much grain people could eat
27937.e: Rich Romans used huge areas of state land. The law limited how much of it one person could have. Anything above that was to be shared out among poor citizens.
27937.m: The land law limited the ownership of state land.

27938.q: How did Tiberius Gracchus meet his end in 133 BC?
a: He was beaten to death by senators and their supporters.
He retired to a country estate.
He fell in a battle against Carthage.
27938.e: Opponents in the Senate accused him of wanting to rule alone. A group of senators and their helpers beat him and many of his supporters to death.
27938.m: Tiberius Gracchus was killed by political opponents.

27939.q: What did a grain law of Gaius Gracchus provide for the citizens of Rome?
27939.e: Gaius Gracchus made sure that citizens in Rome could buy grain at a low, fixed price. This made him very popular with the poor.
27939.m: Gaius Gracchus had grain sold cheaply to citizens.

27940.q: Whose support did the Gracchi mainly rely on for their politics?
27940.e: The Gracchi had their laws passed by the people’s assembly. Many senators were against them because they feared for their property and their power.
27940.m: The Gracchi relied on the ordinary people.

27941.q: Which people did Spartacus come from?
27941.e: Spartacus was a Thracian from the area of today’s Bulgaria. He was taken prisoner and sold as a slave.

27942.q: How did the revolt of Spartacus end?
a: The Romans defeated the army and Spartacus fell
Rome gave all slaves their freedom
27942.e: In 71 BC Crassus defeated the army in southern Italy, and Spartacus fell in battle. Pompey then caught those who fled and also claimed the glory.
27942.m: The revolt of Spartacus was crushed by the Romans.

27943.q: From which city did Spartacus and other gladiators break out in 73 BC?
27943.e: Spartacus and about 70 gladiators escaped from a gladiator school in Capua. With kitchen knives and captured weapons they fought their way free.
27943.m: The revolt of Spartacus began in Capua.

27944.q: Onto which mountain did Spartacus and his people retreat at the start of the revolt?
27944.e: The rebels hid on Vesuvius. According to tradition, they escaped the Romans by climbing down a cliff on ropes made from vines.
27944.m: The rebels gathered around Spartacus on Vesuvius.

27945.q: Roughly how big did Spartacus’ army become?
a: Several tens of thousands of people
27945.e: More and more slaves and poor people joined Spartacus. Ancient sources give figures of 70,000 to over 100,000.
27945.m: Spartacus led an army of several tens of thousands of people.

27946.q: Which Roman general crushed the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BC?
27946.e: Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated the army of Spartacus in southern Italy. Spartacus fell in this battle.
27946.m: Crassus ended the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BC.

27947.q: After the revolt, what happened to about 6000 captured rebels?
a: They were crucified along the Via Appia.
They were sent back to Thrace.
27947.e: As a warning, the prisoners were crucified along the Via Appia between Capua and Rome. This was meant to stop other slaves from rebelling.
27947.m: 6000 rebels were crucified along the Via Appia.

27948.q: What was Marcus Tullius Cicero mainly famous for?
a: As a charioteer in the circus
27948.e: Cicero is seen as the greatest speaker of Rome. His speeches, letters and philosophical writings are still read in Latin lessons today.
27948.m: Cicero was Rome’s most famous speaker.

27949.q: Which high office did Cicero hold in Rome in 63 BC?
27949.e: The consuls were the highest officials of the Roman Republic. There were no emperors yet at that time.

27950.q: What did Cicero uncover as consul?
27950.e: Lucius Sergius Catilina was planning to overthrow the government. Cicero exposed him with famous speeches in the Senate.

27951.q: What does Cicero’s famous cry “O tempora, o mores!” mean?
a: O the times, O the customs!
27951.e: With it, Cicero complained about the decline of morals in Rome. The cry is still quoted today.
27951.m: “O tempora, o mores!” means “O the times, O the customs!”.

27952.q: What was special about Cicero’s rise to the highest office in Rome?
a: Nobody in his family had held a high office before him
He was only twelve years old
He had been a slave before
He was elected by the people of Athens
27952.e: Such a newcomer was called a “homo novus” in Rome, a “new man”. Cicero came from a family of knights from Arpinum.
27952.m: Cicero was the first in his family to hold a high office.

27953.q: After speeches by Demosthenes and Cicero, what is a fierce speech of attack still called today?
27953.e: Demosthenes gave speeches against King Philip, and Cicero used the name for his speeches against Mark Antony. That is where the word “philippic” comes from.
27953.m: A fierce speech of attack is called a philippic.

27954.q: Who had Cicero killed in 43 BC?
27954.e: Mark Antony put Cicero on the list of enemies of the state. Soldiers killed him as he tried to flee.
27954.m: Cicero was killed on the orders of Mark Antony.

27955.q: Which title of honour did Cicero receive after saving Rome from a conspiracy?
27955.e: After the conspiracy of Catilina was crushed, Cicero was called “pater patriae”, Father of the Fatherland. Later the emperors also bore this title.
27955.m: Cicero was called “Father of the Fatherland”.

27956.q: Which three men formed the First Triumvirate?
27956.e: Caesar, Pompey and Crassus made a secret alliance. Together they pushed through their interests against the Senate.
27956.m: The First Triumvirate was made up of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.

27957.q: What did Caesar, Pompey and Crassus want to achieve with their alliance?
a: To push through their aims against the Senate
To give the slaves their freedom
27957.e: The three powerful men helped one another. In this way, from 60 BC they pushed through their interests against the Senate.
27957.m: The First Triumvirate helped three men get their way against the Senate.

27958.e: The word comes from the Latin “tres viri”, three men. It means an alliance or office held by three people.
27958.m: A triumvirate is an alliance of three men.

27959.q: How did Pompey strengthen his alliance with Caesar?
27959.e: In 59 BC Pompey married Caesar’s daughter Julia. Her death in 54 BC weakened the bond between the two men.
27959.m: A marriage closely linked Pompey with Caesar.

27960.q: What was the First Triumvirate in Rome?
a: An alliance of three powerful politicians
27960.e: Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an alliance in 60 BC. In 56 BC they renewed it in the town of Luca.
27960.m: The First Triumvirate was an alliance of three politicians.

27961.q: What brought the First Triumvirate to an end in 53 BC?
27961.e: Crassus wanted to win glory in the East and fell fighting against the Parthians. After that, only Caesar and Pompey faced each other.
27961.m: With the death of Crassus, the First Triumvirate fell apart.

27962.q: What was Marcus Licinius Crassus especially well known for in Rome?
27962.e: Crassus was thought to be the richest man in Rome. Among other things, he made money from land and houses in the city.
27962.m: Crassus was the richest man in ancient Rome.

a: A small river in northern Italy
27963.e: The Rubicon is a small river in north-eastern Italy. In the Roman Republic it was an important border.
27963.m: The Rubicon is a small river in northern Italy.

27964.q: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon with his soldiers in 49 BC?
27964.e: Caesar came from Gaul with his troops. Crossing the Rubicon started a civil war in Rome.
27964.m: Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC.

27965.q: Into which sea does the Rubicon flow?
27965.e: The Rubicon flows north of Rimini and into the Adriatic. For a long time it was disputed exactly where the ancient Rubicon ran.
27965.m: The Rubicon flows into the Adriatic.

27966.q: According to ancient sources, with how many legions did Caesar cross the Rubicon?
27966.e: Caesar only had the 13th Legion with him. His other troops were still in Gaul, but he still dared to advance quickly.
27966.m: Caesar dared to cross the Rubicon with just one legion.

27967.q: Why was crossing the Rubicon with troops such a serious act?
a: A governor was not allowed to march into Italy with his army.
The river was thought to be the home of the gods.
It was the border with the Parthian Empire.
Bridges over the Rubicon were forbidden.
27967.e: A general had to leave his army behind at the border of his province. Anyone who entered Italy with an army was practically declaring war on the state.
27967.m: Crossing the Rubicon with an army meant civil war.

27968.q: What does the saying “to cross the Rubicon” mean today?
a: To make a decision that cannot be undone
To set off on a journey abroad
To only just pass an exam
27968.e: Someone who crosses the Rubicon makes a decision with no way back. The saying recalls Caesar’s decision.
27968.m: Once you cross the Rubicon, there is no going back.

27969.q: Who was Caesar’s great opponent in the civil war after the Rubicon?
27969.e: Pompey had once been Caesar’s ally. In the civil war Caesar defeated him in 48 BC, after which Pompey fled to Egypt.
27969.m: In the civil war, Caesar defeated Pompey.

27970.q: Which day is meant by the “Ides of March”?
27970.e: The Romans called the middle of the month the Ides. In March this was the 15th day. On this day in 44 BC Caesar was murdered.
27970.m: The Ides of March are 15 March.

27971.q: What did the conspirators want to celebrate with a coin after Caesar’s murder?
27971.e: One of the conspirators had a coin made showing two daggers and a cap of liberty. It presented the murder as freeing Rome from a sole ruler.
27971.m: The conspirators celebrated Caesar’s murder as the liberation of Rome.

27972.q: What did the Roman state declare Caesar to be after his death?
27972.e: After his death, Caesar was officially declared a god. Later a temple was built for him in the Forum.
27972.m: Caesar was declared a god after his death.

a: At a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey
In his house on the Palatine
On a boat on the Tiber
27973.e: The Senate meeting took place in a hall next to the Theatre of Pompey. Caesar is said to have died at the foot of a statue of Pompey.
27973.m: Caesar was stabbed during a meeting of the Senate.

27974.q: What did the conspirators kill Caesar with?
27974.e: The conspirators hid daggers under their robes. At the Senate meeting they stabbed Caesar.

27975.q: Which title had Caesar taken shortly before his murder?
a: Tribune of the people for ever
27975.e: At the beginning of 44 BC Caesar became dictator for life. Many senators feared that he wanted to rule like a king.
27975.m: As dictator for life, Caesar seemed like a king to many senators.

27976.q: According to tradition, who warned Caesar about the Ides of March?
27976.e: The seer Spurinna is said to have warned Caesar of a danger that would come by the Ides of March at the latest. In Shakespeare the line is “Beware the Ides of March”.
27976.m: A seer warned Caesar about the Ides of March.

27977.q: After Caesar’s death, who finally became sole ruler and the first emperor of Rome?
27977.e: Caesar’s adopted son Octavian defeated his opponents and ruled alone from 27 BC. He called himself Augustus and is seen as the first Roman emperor.
27977.m: After Caesar, Augustus became the first emperor of Rome.

27978.q: In which year AD was Pompeii destroyed by a volcanic eruption?
27978.e: In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii under a thick layer of ash and pumice.

27979.q: Which natural event had already badly damaged Pompeii about 17 years before the volcanic eruption?
27979.e: Around AD 62 a strong earthquake shook the area. Many buildings were still being repaired when the city was buried.
27979.m: Even before the eruption, an earthquake had badly damaged Pompeii.

27980.q: Near which modern large city is Pompeii?
27980.e: Pompeii lies in Campania in southern Italy, about 25 kilometres south-east of Naples.

27983.q: How did archaeologists make the body shapes of the victims of Pompeii visible again?
a: They poured plaster into hollow spaces
They built figures out of wood
27983.e: The bodies decayed in the ash and left hollow spaces. From 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli had these filled with plaster.
27983.m: The plaster casts show the shapes of the victims of Pompeii.

27984.q: Why is Pompeii still so well preserved today?
a: It was repaired again and again
27984.e: The layer of ash and pumice, several metres thick, protected houses, wall paintings and everyday objects for almost 1700 years.
27984.m: Under ash and pumice, Pompeii stayed almost unchanged.

27985.q: What can visitors see in Pompeii today?
a: Roman streets, houses and wall paintings
An active lava lake in the middle of the town
27985.e: Archaeologists have dug up a large part of the city. You can walk through old streets and look at houses, bakeries and wall paintings.
27985.m: In Pompeii you can visit a Roman town.

27987.q: Apart from gladiator fights, what else was shown in the Colosseum?
27987.e: In animal hunts, people fought against lions, bears and other wild animals. Chariot races, on the other hand, took place in the Circus Maximus.
27987.m: There were also fights with wild animals in the Colosseum.

27988.q: Where does the Colosseum probably get its name from?
a: From a huge statue next to it
27988.e: Next to the building stood a huge statue, the Colossus of Nero. Later the amphitheatre was named the Colosseum after it.
27988.m: The Colosseum is named after a huge statue.

27989.q: Roughly how high is the outer wall of the Colosseum?
27989.e: The Colosseum is about 48 metres high, 188 metres long and 156 metres wide. It was the largest amphitheatre in the Roman Empire.
27989.m: The wall of the Colosseum is about 50 metres high.

27990.q: What were the fighters called who fought each other in front of an audience in the Colosseum?
27990.e: Gladiators were mostly slaves, prisoners of war or condemned criminals who were trained for the fights in special schools.

27991.q: How were the spectators in the Colosseum protected from the sun?
27991.e: Sailors stretched huge lengths of cloth above the seats. This awning was called the velarium.
27991.m: An awning protected the spectators in the Colosseum.

27992.q: What was underneath the arena of the Colosseum?
a: Passages and cages for animals and fighters
A water tank for the whole of Rome
27992.e: Animals and fighters waited under the arena. With lifts and trapdoors they appeared in the arena by surprise.
27992.m: Under the arena there were passages, cages and lifts.

27993.q: How did the large amount of water get into the big baths in the city of Rome?
27993.e: Aqueducts carried fresh spring water into the city on a gentle slope, often over many kilometres. Part of it supplied the baths.
27993.m: Aqueducts brought the water to the baths.

27994.q: What was the room with the cold bath in the Roman baths called?
27994.e: The word comes from the Latin “frigidus”, meaning cold. People cooled off there after sweating.
27994.m: In the frigidarium you took a cold bath.

27995.q: What is the Roman underfloor heating that heated the baths called?
27995.e: Under the floor, resting on small brick pillars, hot air flowed from a furnace and warmed the floor and walls.
27995.m: The hypocaust was a Roman underfloor heating system.

27996.q: How big were the Baths of Caracalla in Rome?
a: Huge, over a thousand people could bathe at the same time
Just one pool for ten people
Just big enough for the emperor alone
27996.e: The Baths of Caracalla were finished around AD 216. There was room for over a thousand bathers at the same time. Today the ruins are used as an opera stage in summer.
27996.m: The Baths of Caracalla were a huge bathing complex.

27997.q: Where did visitors to the Roman baths put their clothes?
a: In niches in the wall of the changing room
Nowhere, they bathed in their clothes
27997.e: In the changing room, the apodyterium, there were niches in the walls for clothes. Often a slave kept watch so that nothing was stolen.
27997.m: In the changing room the Romans put their clothes in wall niches.

27998.q: What did the Romans use a strigil for in the baths?
a: To scrape off oil and sweat
27998.e: Soap was hardly known. People rubbed themselves with oil and scraped it off again, along with the dirt, using the curved metal scraper.
27998.m: The strigil was used to clean the skin.

27999.q: What was the palaestra in a Roman bath used for?
27999.e: The palaestra was an open courtyard where people could wrestle, run or play ball before bathing.
27999.m: In the palaestra people did sport before bathing.

28000.q: What do you mainly see in the Roman Forum today?
28000.e: Columns, arches and remains of walls survive from what was once the centre of Rome. Many tourists visit the ruins.
28000.m: Today there are ruins in the Roman Forum.

28001.q: The Roman Forum lies in a hollow between hills. On how many hills is ancient Rome said to have been built?
28001.e: Rome is also called the “City of Seven Hills”. The Forum lies between two of them, the Capitol and the Palatine.
28001.m: Rome is the city of seven hills.

28002.q: What were the large halls in the Roman Forum called, where trials were held and business was done?
28002.e: Well-known examples are the Basilica Julia and the Basilica Aemilia. Later, Christian churches took over this type of building.
28002.m: Justice was done in the basilica at the Forum.

28003.q: What was the Roman Forum in ancient Rome?
a: The most important square in the city
28003.e: In the Forum the Romans met to trade, for courts, speeches and festivals. Temples and halls stood all around it.
28003.m: The Roman Forum was the centre of ancient Rome.

28004.q: What does a triumphal arch such as the Arch of Titus in the Roman Forum commemorate?
28004.e: The Arch of Titus celebrates the capture of Jerusalem in the year 70. A relief shows soldiers carrying the seven-branched lampstand from the Temple.

28005.q: What was the meaning of the Golden Milestone that Augustus had set up in the Roman Forum?
a: It was seen as the starting point of the roads
It marked the grave of Romulus
It served as an altar for offerings
28005.e: The gilded stone is said to have shown the distances to important cities of the empire. It is often linked with the saying “All roads lead to Rome”.
28005.m: The Golden Milestone was seen as the centre of the Roman roads.

28006.q: What was the Rostra in the Roman Forum?
28006.e: The platform was decorated with the bronze beaks of captured ships, called “rostra” in Latin. From here, politicians spoke to the people.
28006.m: Politicians made their speeches from the Rostra.

28008.q: Why were the flats on the upper floors of an insula usually cheaper?
a: No water and a high risk of fire
They had windows that were too big
28008.e: Water had to be carried up, and in a fire you were trapped at the top. The buildings were often badly built.
28008.m: In an insula, the poorest people often lived right at the top.

28009.e: The domus was a town house for a wealthy family and their slaves. It faced inwards and had hardly any windows onto the street.
28009.m: A domus was the house of a rich family.

28010.q: What was the central reception room of a domus with an opening in the roof called?
28010.e: The master of the house received his guests in the atrium. Light and rain came in through the opening in the roof.
28010.m: The atrium was the heart of the domus.

28011.q: What was the impluvium in a Roman domus used for?
28011.e: The shallow pool lay under the opening in the roof of the atrium and caught the rainwater.

28012.q: What does the mosaic inscription “Cave canem” at the entrance to a house in Pompeii mean?
28012.e: The mosaic in the House of the Tragic Poet shows a dog on a chain. It warned visitors like a sign does today.
28012.m: “Cave canem” warned people about the dog.

28013.q: How did rich Romans eat at a feast in their domus?
28013.e: In the dining room, the triclinium, there were three couches around a table. People ate half lying down, leaning on their left elbow.
28013.m: Rich Romans ate half lying down.

28014.q: Which script that we use today in English goes back to the Romans?
28014.e: The Romans took their alphabet from the Etruscans and the Greeks. Today it is the most widely used script in the world.
28014.m: Our alphabet comes from the Romans.

28015.q: What are the languages that developed from Latin called?
28015.e: Languages such as Italian, Spanish and Portuguese developed from spoken Latin.
28015.m: The Romance languages come from Latin.

28016.q: Which language in the Grisons developed from the Latin of the Romans?
28016.e: Romansh developed from the Latin spoken by Roman soldiers, officials and settlers in Raetia. It is one of the four national languages of Switzerland.

28017.q: What does the Latin abbreviation “etc.”, which we still use today, mean?
28017.e: “Etc.” stands for “et cetera”, literally “and the rest”. We use it at the end of lists.
28017.m: The abbreviation etc. means and so on.

28018.q: Apart from Latin, which language was the most important common language in the east of the Roman Empire?
28018.e: Since Alexander the Great, Greek had been spoken in the eastern Mediterranean. The Romans kept it there as the language of government and education.
28018.m: In the east of the empire people mainly spoke Greek.

28019.q: What is the Latin that ordinary people spoke in everyday life called?
28019.e: “Vulgus” means the common people. New languages later developed from this everyday spoken language.
28019.m: The people spoke Vulgar Latin in everyday life.

28020.q: In which language are the scientific names of animals and plants formed?
28020.e: Since Carl Linnaeus, every species has been given a two-part Latin name, for example Homo sapiens. This way researchers all over the world understand it.
28020.m: Scientific names of animals and plants are Latin.

28021.q: Which number is written with the Roman numerals XIV?
28021.e: X is 10 and IV is 4, because the I in front of the V is taken away. So 10 + 4 = 14.

28022.e: The numeral L has the value 50. It comes between X for 10 and C for 100.

28023.q: Which year is written as MMXXVI?
28023.e: MM is 2000, XX is 20 and VI is 6. Together that makes 2000 + 20 + 6 = 2026.
28023.m: The year 2026 is written MMXXVI in Roman numerals.

28024.q: What value does the Roman numeral D have?
28024.e: D stands for 500. The sign came from half of an old sign for 1000.

28025.e: If a smaller numeral comes before a bigger one, it is taken away: C is 100, X is 10, so 100 minus 10 = 90.
28025.m: XC is the Roman way of writing 90.

28026.q: How do you write the number 9 in Roman numerals?
28026.e: You take I away from X: 10 minus 1 = 9. XI, on the other hand, would be 11.
28026.m: The number 9 is written IX in Roman numerals.

28027.q: Which number does not have its own sign in the Roman number system?
28027.e: The Romans did not need a zero, because their numerals have no place values. Zero came to Europe later via India and the Arab world.
28027.m: The Romans had no sign for zero.

28028.q: Which number is written as CXXIII?
28028.e: C is 100, XX is 20 and III is 3. Together that makes 100 + 20 + 3 = 123.
28028.m: CXXIII is the Roman way of writing 123.

28030.q: Which group did Nero blame for the fire of Rome and have persecuted?
28030.e: According to the historian Tacitus, Nero put the blame on the Christians to draw rumours away from himself.
28030.m: After the fire, Nero had the Christians persecuted.

28031.q: What was the name of the splendid palace that Nero had built after the fire?
28031.e: In Latin it was called the Domus Aurea. The huge palace with its park was built on land that had been destroyed in the fire.
28031.m: Nero’s palace was called the Golden House.

28032.q: Who mainly helped Nero to become Roman emperor?
28032.e: His mother Agrippina married Emperor Claudius and made sure that Nero was adopted. That is how he came to power.
28032.m: Nero’s mother brought him to power.

28033.q: What was Seneca, the teacher and adviser of the young Nero?
28033.e: Seneca was a famous philosopher and writer. He shaped Nero’s first years in power but later fell out of favour.
28033.m: Nero’s teacher Seneca was a philosopher.

28034.q: What followed in the Roman Empire after Nero’s death?
a: A year with four emperors one after another
The end of the Roman Empire
A hundred years without a ruler
28034.e: Nero had no successor. In AD 69 several generals fought for power, and in the end Vespasian won.
28034.m: After Nero came the Year of the Four Emperors.

28035.q: According to a rumour, what is Nero said to have done during the great fire of Rome?
28035.e: Even ancient writers reported the rumour that Nero sang a song during the fire. Whether it is true is not certain; he was not even in Rome at the start.
28035.m: According to a rumour, Nero sang while Rome burned.

28036.q: How did Trajan become Roman emperor?
a: He was a son of Emperor Nero
28036.e: Emperor Nerva adopted the successful general Trajan. After Nerva’s death in the year 98, Trajan became emperor.
28036.m: Trajan became emperor because Nerva had adopted him.

28037.q: From which province did Trajan, the first Roman emperor not from Italy, come?
28037.e: Trajan was born in Italica, a Roman town near today’s Seville in Spain.
28037.m: Trajan came from the province of Hispania.

28038.q: Which area in today’s Romania did Trajan conquer in two wars?
28038.e: After wars in the years 101 to 102 and 105 to 106, Dacia became a Roman province. The land was rich in gold.
28038.m: Trajan made Dacia a Roman province.

28039.q: What does Trajan’s Column in Rome show?
a: Pictures of Trajan’s wars in Dacia
A list of all the emperors
A map of the Roman Empire
28039.e: A band of pictures carved in stone winds around the whole column. It shows scenes from the wars against the Dacians. Since 1587 a figure of the apostle Peter has stood at the top.
28039.m: Trajan’s Column tells the story of Trajan’s wars in pictures.

28040.q: What did the Romans think of Emperor Trajan?
a: They thought he was one of the best emperors
They thought he was the cruellest emperor
They removed him after a year
28040.e: The Senate gave him the title “Optimus Princeps”, best ruler. Later emperors were greeted with the wish that they would be better than Trajan.
28040.m: The Romans saw Trajan as the best ruler.

28041.q: Who became Trajan’s successor in the year 117?
28041.e: Trajan is said to have adopted him shortly before his death. In this way power passed to his relative from Italica.
28041.m: Trajan was followed by Emperor Hadrian.

28042.q: Which group of emperors is Trajan counted among?
28042.e: These emperors usually chose their successor by adopting a capable man rather than by birth.
28042.m: Trajan belongs to the adoptive emperors.

28044.e: Emperor Hadrian had the wall built from the year 122. Roman soldiers put it up in just a few years.

28045.q: What are the small guard posts that stood about every Roman mile along Hadrian’s Wall called?
28045.e: A small group of soldiers lived in each milecastle. A gate allowed controlled passage to the north.
28045.m: There were milecastles at regular distances along Hadrian’s Wall.

28046.q: Roughly how long was Hadrian’s Wall?
28046.e: The wall stretched about 120 kilometres from the east coast to the west coast of Britain. In this way it closed off the whole island at its narrowest point.
28046.m: Hadrian’s Wall stretched right across the island of Britain.

28047.q: Which building with a huge dome did Emperor Hadrian have rebuilt in Rome?
28047.e: The Pantheon was a temple for all the gods. Its concrete dome is still the largest unreinforced dome in the world.
28047.m: Emperor Hadrian had the Pantheon rebuilt.

28048.q: Which building in Rome was originally the tomb of Emperor Hadrian?
28048.e: The round mausoleum by the Tiber was later turned into a fortress for the popes and is now called Castel Sant’Angelo.
28048.m: Castel Sant’Angelo was once Hadrian’s tomb.

28049.q: Which fashion did Emperor Hadrian make popular among Roman men?
28049.e: Hadrian was the first emperor to wear a full beard all the time. Many of his successors followed his example.
28049.m: With Hadrian, beards became fashionable among emperors.

28050.e: The Limes was made up of banks, ditches, fences, watchtowers and forts. It protected the border of the empire.
28050.m: The Limes was the fortified border of the Roman Empire.

28051.q: Between which two rivers did the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes run?
28051.e: The Limes closed the gap between the two rivers, which otherwise already formed a natural border.
28051.m: The Limes linked the Rhine and the Danube.

28052.q: Roughly how long was the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes?
28052.e: At about 550 kilometres, it is one of the largest archaeological monuments in Europe. It ran through what is now southern Germany.
28052.m: The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes was about 550 kilometres long.

28053.q: What do you call a fortified camp for Roman soldiers on the border?
28053.e: Forts were rectangular camps with a wall, gates and towers. The troops who guarded the border lived there.
28053.m: The border soldiers lived in a fort.

28054.q: Which distinction does the Limes hold today?
a: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site
It is a world-record hiking trail
28054.e: Since 2005 the Limes has been part of the World Heritage Site “Frontiers of the Roman Empire”, together with Hadrian’s Wall in Great Britain.
28054.m: The Limes is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

28055.q: What can you visit today at some places along the Limes?
28055.e: At several places, watchtowers and forts have been rebuilt, for example the Saalburg near Bad Homburg. There are museums about Roman times there.
28055.m: Today there are rebuilt towers and forts along the Limes.

28056.q: Why did the Romans give up the Limes in Germania around AD 260?
a: They could no longer hold it against attacks
They had defeated all the Germanic peoples
The Germanic peoples bought it from them
28056.e: In the crisis of the empire in the 3rd century, there was a lack of soldiers and money. The border was moved back to the Rhine, the Iller and the Danube.
28056.m: Around AD 260 the Romans could no longer hold the Limes.

28057.q: What does the Latin expression “Pax Romana” mean?
28057.e: “Pax” means peace. It refers to a long period in which there were hardly any wars inside the empire.

28058.q: With which ruler did the Pax Romana begin?
28058.e: After the end of the civil wars, Rome’s first emperor led the empire into a long period of peace.
28058.m: The Pax Romana began with Emperor Augustus.

28059.q: Roughly how long did the Pax Romana last?
28059.e: The period of peace began in the late 1st century BC and lasted until the late 2nd century AD.
28059.m: The Pax Romana lasted about two centuries.

28060.q: What did the Senate in Rome have built in honour of the peace under Augustus?
28060.e: The altar of peace is called the Ara Pacis in Latin and was dedicated in 9 BC. Today it stands in a modern museum building in Rome.
28060.m: The Ara Pacis is the altar of peace of Augustus.

28061.q: Thanks to the Pax Romana, what especially flourished throughout the empire?
28061.e: Safe roads and seas, a shared currency and little war made it easier to exchange goods.
28061.m: Thanks to the peace, trade flourished in the empire.

28062.q: What happened to the doors of the Temple of Janus in Rome when there was peace throughout the empire?
28062.e: In times of war the doors stood open. Augustus had them closed several times, which happened very rarely.
28062.m: Closed doors at the Temple of Janus showed there was peace.

28063.q: With the death of which emperor in the year 180 is the Pax Romana usually said to end?
28063.e: Marcus Aurelius already had to fight many wars on the borders. After his death a more troubled time began.
28063.m: The Pax Romana ended with Marcus Aurelius.

28064.q: What did the Milan agreement of 313 under Constantine allow the Christians to do?
28064.e: The agreement gave everyone in the empire freedom of religion. This largely ended the great persecutions of Christians.
28064.m: From 313, Christians were allowed to practise their faith freely.

28066.q: According to tradition, which sign did Constantine have painted on his soldiers’ shields?
28066.e: The sign is made of the Greek letters chi and rho, the first letters of “Christ” in Greek.
28066.m: Constantine’s soldiers carried the Chi-Rho symbol of Christ.

28067.q: Who met at the Council of Nicaea in 325 at Constantine’s invitation?
28067.e: At the first council for the whole Church, the bishops agreed on a shared creed.
28067.m: In 325 Constantine called the bishops to Nicaea.

28068.q: Who proclaimed Constantine emperor in the year 306?
28068.e: Constantine’s father, an emperor, had died in Britain. The troops there immediately proclaimed his son as successor.

28069.q: What metal was the solidus, Emperor Constantine’s important coin, made of?
28069.e: The solidus had a fixed weight of gold and kept its value for centuries. The word soldier goes back to its name, because soldiers were paid with it.
28069.m: The solidus was a gold coin.

28071.q: Into which two parts was the Roman Empire divided in 395?
a: A Western and an Eastern Roman Empire
A northern and a southern empire
28071.e: After the death of Emperor Theodosius, each of his two sons received one half. This is how the Western and Eastern Roman Empires came about.
28071.m: In 395 the Roman Empire was divided into West and East.

28072.q: Which city was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire?
28072.e: Constantinople lay on the Bosporus between Europe and Asia. Today the city is called Istanbul.
28072.m: Constantinople was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.

28073.q: Which part of the Roman Empire lasted longer after the division?
a: Both ended in the same year
28073.e: The Western Empire ended in AD 476. The Eastern Empire, however, lasted almost another thousand years until 1453.
28073.m: The Eastern Empire outlived the Western Empire by almost a thousand years.

28074.q: In which year did the Western Roman Empire end?
28074.e: In 476 the Germanic army leader Odoacer removed the last Western Roman emperor. This was the end of the Western Empire.
28074.m: The Western Roman Empire ended in AD 476.

28075.q: Which religion did Emperor Theodosius I declare the state religion in 380?
a: The religion of the Roman gods
28075.e: With a decree he required the people of the empire to follow the Christian faith. Later he also banned the old cults of sacrifice.
28075.m: Under Theodosius I, Christianity became the state religion.

28076.q: In which modern city is the famous domed church of Hagia Sophia?
28076.e: The Hagia Sophia was built in the 6th century in Constantinople, today’s Istanbul. For a long time it was the largest church in the world.
28076.m: The Hagia Sophia is in Istanbul.

28077.q: By which other name is the Eastern Roman Empire also known today?
28077.e: The name goes back to Byzantion, the old Greek name of the capital. But the people called themselves Romans.
28077.m: The Eastern Roman Empire is also called the Byzantine Empire.

28078.q: In which modern country are the ruins of Mohenjo-daro?
28078.e: Mohenjo-daro lies on the Indus in today’s Pakistan. It was one of the largest cities of the Indus civilisation.

28079.q: What threatens the mud bricks of Mohenjo-daro today?
28079.e: Salty groundwater rises into the old bricks and makes them crumble. The ruins have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.

28080.q: Which famous structure was excavated at Mohenjo-daro?
28080.e: The Great Bath is a watertight pool made of fired bricks and sealed with bitumen. It was probably used for ritual washing.
28080.m: The famous Great Bath is at Mohenjo-daro.

28081.q: What was Mohenjo-daro especially advanced in for its time?
28081.e: Many houses had bathrooms and toilets whose waste water flowed into covered drains along the streets. Hardly anywhere else had a sewer system like this at the time.
28081.m: Mohenjo-daro already had a clever drainage system.

28082.q: What are the cities of the Indus civilisation, such as Mohenjo-daro, famous for?
28082.e: The cities of the Indus civilisation had straight streets, brick houses and covered drains for waste water. That was very advanced for their time.
28082.m: Indus cities had planned streets and drains.

28083.q: Roughly how old are the great cities of the Indus civilisation?
28083.e: The great cities of the Indus civilisation flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BC. So they are about as old as the pyramids in Egypt.
28083.m: The Indus civilisation is about as old as the pyramids.

28084.q: What is still an unsolved mystery of the Indus civilisation?
28084.e: Thousands of short inscriptions in the Indus script are known, mainly on seals. So far nobody has deciphered them.
28084.m: The Indus script has still not been deciphered.

28085.q: Which typical finds from the Indus civilisation often show animals such as a unicorn-like bull?
28085.e: The small square soapstone seals show animals and written signs. Traders probably pressed them into clay to mark goods.
28085.m: The Indus people marked goods with small soapstone seals.

28086.q: In which modern country did the Maurya Empire mainly lie?
28086.e: The Maurya Empire arose around 320 BC and covered almost all of India. It was the first great Indian empire.
28086.m: The Maurya Empire lay in India.

28087.q: On which great river did the capital of the Maurya Empire lie?
28087.e: The capital Pataliputra lay on the Ganges, where the city of Patna is today. At that time it was one of the largest cities in the world.
28087.m: The capital of the Mauryas lay on the Ganges.

28088.q: Which religion did Emperor Ashoka promote in the Maurya Empire?
28088.e: After a bloody war, Ashoka turned to Buddhism. He sent out monks and had pillars with inscriptions put up.

28089.q: Which animals from the Maurya period appear on India’s national emblem today?
28089.e: The emblem shows four lions sitting back to back on top of a pillar. It is based on a pillar from the time of Emperor Ashoka.
28089.m: India’s emblem shows lions from the Maurya period.

28090.q: Which religion did the Indian emperor Ashoka turn to after a bloody war?
28090.e: Ashoka regretted the suffering his war had caused. He became a Buddhist and called for non-violence.
28090.m: Ashoka became a Buddhist after a war.

28091.q: How did Ashoka make his rules and teachings known throughout the empire?
a: He had them carved into rocks and pillars
He had them printed on silk
He only had them announced by word of mouth
28091.e: The so-called Edicts of Ashoka are on rock faces and stone pillars all over South Asia. They call for non-violence, tolerance and respect for animals.
28091.m: Ashoka had his edicts carved in stone.

28092.q: Which symbol of Ashoka can be seen in the middle of the Indian flag today?
a: A crescent moon with a star
28092.e: The blue Ashoka Chakra on India’s flag is a wheel with 24 spokes. It stands for law and teaching.
28092.m: The wheel on India’s flag is called the Ashoka Chakra.

28093.q: Where did Ashoka send his son Mahinda to spread Buddhism?
28093.e: In the 3rd century BC Mahinda brought the Buddha’s teaching to Sri Lanka. Buddhism is still the largest religion there today.
28093.m: Ashoka’s son Mahinda brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka.

28094.q: According to tradition, how old was the Buddha when he died?
28094.e: According to tradition, the Buddha died at about 80 in Kushinagar. His death is seen as his entry into final nirvana.
28094.m: According to tradition, the Buddha lived to about 80.

28095.q: What does the Buddhist goal “nirvana” literally mean?
28095.e: Nirvana literally means blowing out, as with a flame. It refers to the end of greed, hatred and ignorance, and so the end of suffering.
28095.m: Nirvana means the blowing out of suffering.

28096.q: Who was Siddhartha Gautama before his life as a wandering teacher?
28096.e: Siddhartha was the son of a ruler from the Shakya clan. He grew up in luxury but left the palace at the age of 29.
28096.m: The Buddha was a prince who left his palace.

28097.q: According to legend, which four encounters moved Siddhartha to leave the palace?
a: An old man, a sick man, a dead man and a holy man
A beggar, a child, a trader and a soldier
A king, a priest, a farmer and a thief
A teacher, a mother, a doctor and a hunter
28097.e: On the “Four Sights”, Siddhartha saw old age, sickness and death. The holy man showed him a way to seek freedom from suffering.
28097.m: Old age, sickness and death showed the Buddha the suffering of people.

28098.q: Under which tree did Siddhartha reach enlightenment at Bodh Gaya?
28098.e: He meditated under a sacred fig tree until he was enlightened. Since then this tree has been called the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening.
28098.m: The Buddha was enlightened under a Bodhi tree.

28099.q: What did the Buddha do after his enlightenment?
a: He travelled around and taught others his way
He became king of a great empire
He lived alone in a cave for ever
He became a trader on the Silk Road
28099.e: After his enlightenment, the Buddha travelled through northern India for about 45 years, teaching. He gave his first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath.
28099.m: After his enlightenment, the Buddha taught for many years.

28100.q: What are the Buddha’s “Four Noble Truths” about?
a: Suffering and how to overcome it
The four points of the compass
28100.e: The truths say: there is suffering, it has a cause, it can end, and there is a way to get there. They form the heart of the Buddha’s teaching.
28100.m: The Four Noble Truths are about suffering and its end.

28101.q: According to the Buddha, what is the path that leads out of suffering called?
28101.e: The Eightfold Path includes, among other things, right view, right speech and right action. It is a middle way between luxury and strict self-denial.
28101.m: According to the Buddha, the Eightfold Path leads out of suffering.

28102.q: Which work made Confucius famous above all?
28102.e: Confucius taught many students and also took in those from ordinary families. He is seen as one of China’s first private teachers.
28102.m: Confucius became famous as a teacher.

28103.q: Roughly how many years ago did Confucius live?
28103.e: Confucius lived from about 551 to 479 BC. That is about 2500 years ago.

28104.q: Which country did Confucius come from?
28104.e: Confucius was born in the small state of Lu in eastern China. His teaching still shapes China today.

28105.q: Who wrote down the sayings of Confucius after his death?
28105.e: His students collected his sayings and conversations in a book. It is one of the most important writings of China.
28105.m: The students of Confucius wrote down his teachings.

28106.q: Which virtue did Confucius put at the centre of his teaching?
28106.e: Ren means humaneness or kindness towards others. A noble person should show it in everyday life through right behaviour.
28106.m: For Confucius, humaneness is the most important virtue.

28107.q: What is meant by the “filial piety” that Confucius demanded?
28107.e: Children should honour their parents, obey them and look after them in old age. The ancestors should also be honoured.
28107.m: Filial piety means deep respect for parents and ancestors.

28108.q: What stands in many Chinese cities in honour of Confucius?
28108.e: There are temples for Confucius all over China. The largest is in his home town of Qufu, where his grave also lies.
28108.m: There are many temples for Confucius in China.

28109.q: Which rule for life did Confucius teach?
a: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you
28109.e: Confucius taught that you should treat others the way you would like to be treated yourself. Many religions have a similar rule.
28109.m: Confucius taught: treat others the way you want to be treated.

28111.q: How long did the imperial dynasty founded by Qin Shi Huang last?
28111.e: The Qin dynasty ruled from 221 to 206 BC. Shortly after the death of the first emperor, revolts broke out.
28111.m: The Qin dynasty lasted only about 15 years.

28112.q: Roughly what does the title Qin Shi Huang mean?
28112.e: Shi means “first” and Huangdi means “emperor”. He wanted to show that a completely new age was beginning with him.
28112.m: Qin Shi Huang means First Emperor of Qin.

28113.q: What did the coins look like that were used throughout the empire under Qin Shi Huang?
a: Oval with a picture of the emperor
28113.e: The round bronze coin with a square hole was called the ban liang. This shape stayed in use in China for over 2000 years.
28113.m: Chinese coins were round and had a square hole.

28114.q: What did Qin Shi Huang have destroyed in 213 BC to silence criticism?
28114.e: In the burning of the books, mainly the writings of philosophers and history books of other states were destroyed. Books on medicine, farming and fortune-telling were spared.
28114.m: Qin Shi Huang had many books burned.

28115.q: How did Qin Shi Huang rule his empire?
a: With strict laws and harsh punishments
With votes by all the people
With the help of an elected parliament
28115.e: The first emperor relied on clear laws and harsh punishments. Anyone who did not obey them could expect serious consequences.
28115.m: Qin Shi Huang ruled very strictly.

28116.q: What did Qin Shi Huang search for tirelessly towards the end of his life?
28116.e: He sent out scholars and expeditions to find an elixir of life. Even so, he died on a journey in 210 BC.
28116.m: The first emperor searched in vain for eternal life.

28117.q: Which modern name probably goes back to the state of Qin?
28117.e: Many researchers think that the word “China” comes from “Qin” (pronounced “chin”). The Chinese themselves call their country Zhongguo.
28117.m: The name China probably comes from the state of Qin.

28119.q: Near which Chinese city is the Terracotta Army?
28119.e: The pits are at Lintong, east of Xi’an in Shaanxi province.
28119.m: The Terracotta Army is near Xi’an.

28120.q: Roughly how many figures does the Terracotta Army include?
28120.e: Researchers estimate the number of warriors, horses and chariots at about 8000 figures. Many of them have not been dug up yet.
28120.m: The Terracotta Army has about 8000 figures.

28121.e: Terracotta comes from Italian and means baked earth. It refers to fired clay without a glaze.

28122.q: What did the terracotta warriors originally look like?
28122.e: The figures were painted in bright colours. In the air, the paint often flakes off quickly after they are dug up.
28122.m: The terracotta warriors were once brightly painted.

28123.q: What was the Terracotta Army meant for?
a: To protect the emperor in the afterlife
To entertain children in the palace
To serve as an offering to the gods
28123.e: The army guards the tomb of the first emperor of China. It was meant to protect him after his death.
28123.m: The clay warriors were meant to guard the emperor in the afterlife.

28124.q: What is still true today of the emperor’s actual burial mound next to the Terracotta Army?
a: It has not been opened yet
It is a museum you can go into
28124.e: The burial mound has not been excavated so far. People do not want to damage the tomb and are looking for gentle methods.
28124.m: The tomb of the first emperor is still unopened.

28125.q: What stood at regular distances along the Great Wall of China?
28125.e: There were many watchtowers on the wall. From there, soldiers kept a lookout and passed on warning signals.
28125.m: There were many watchtowers on the Great Wall of China.

28126.q: How old are most of the parts of the Great Wall of China that can be seen today?
28126.e: The well-preserved sections made of bricks and stone were mainly built between 1368 and 1644 under the Ming dynasty. Older parts have often fallen into ruin.
28126.m: The best-known parts of the wall are a few hundred years old.

28127.q: What was the Great Wall of China mainly meant to protect against?
28127.e: Nomadic peoples such as the Xiongnu kept raiding Chinese lands. The wall made their raids more difficult.
28127.m: The wall protected China from horse-riding peoples from the north.

28128.q: According to an official survey from 2012, how long are all the sections of the Great Wall of China added together?
28128.e: In 2012 the Chinese authority for cultural heritage came to about 21,196 kilometres. All sections of the wall from different periods were added together.
28128.m: All the sections of the Great Wall of China together are over 20,000 km long.

28129.q: Is it true that you can see the Great Wall of China from the Moon with the naked eye?
28129.e: The wall is very long, but only a few metres wide. From the Moon it cannot be seen with the naked eye.
28129.m: You cannot see the Great Wall of China from the Moon.

28130.q: How did the guards on the Great Wall of China pass on warnings?
28130.e: Signal fires were lit from tower to tower, and during the day the smoke could be seen. In this way a message travelled quickly over long distances.
28130.m: The wall guards warned each other with smoke and fire.

28131.q: What material were many early sections of the Great Wall of China made of?
28131.e: For early walls, earth was filled in layers between boards and pounded firm. This way of building is called rammed earth.
28131.m: Early parts of the wall were made of rammed earth.

28132.q: With which great empire did the Han dynasty in China exist at roughly the same time?
28132.e: The Han ruled from 206 BC to AD 220. During this time the Roman Empire in the West was at its height.
28132.m: The Han dynasty ruled at the same time as the Roman Empire.

28133.q: Which famous trade route to the West came about at the time of the Han dynasty?
28133.e: Trade along the Silk Road began under the Han. Along this route, silk and other goods from China reached the Mediterranean.
28133.m: The Silk Road came about in Han times.

28134.q: Which important invention comes from China at the time of the Han dynasty?
28134.e: Paper was made in China in Han times. Around AD 105 the official Cai Lun improved the way it was made. Gunpowder only came much later.
28134.m: Paper was invented in China in Han times.

28135.q: What do you call a series of rulers from the same family, such as the Han in China?
28135.e: In a dynasty, power is passed on within one family, usually from father to son. The Han dynasty ruled China for over 400 years.
28135.m: A ruling family is called a dynasty.

28136.q: Which teaching did Emperor Wu of Han make the basis of the state?
28136.e: Emperor Wu promoted the teaching of Confucius and founded an academy for future officials. After that, Confucianism shaped China for about 2000 years.
28136.m: Under the Han, Confucianism became the state teaching.

28137.q: Which is China’s largest ethnic group that still bears the name of this dynasty today?
28137.e: China’s largest population group is named after the Han dynasty. Chinese characters are also called hanzi.
28137.m: Most Chinese people call themselves Han after the Han dynasty.

28138.q: How did the earthquake detector from Han times show that an earthquake had happened?
a: A ball fell out of a dragon’s mouth
28138.e: In the year 132 the scholar Zhang Heng built a vessel with eight dragons. During an earthquake, a ball dropped into the mouth of a toad and so showed the direction.
28138.m: In the Han earthquake detector, a ball dropped when there was an earthquake.

28139.q: Why do people speak of the Western and Eastern Han?
a: Because the capital was later further east
Because two emperors ruled at the same time
Because China was split into two countries
Because the Han later moved to Japan
28139.e: The early Han ruled from Chang’an. After a short break, they moved the capital to Luoyang, which lies further east.
28139.m: The Eastern Han ruled from a capital further east.

28140.q: Why is the Silk Road called that?
a: Because valuable silk from China was traded along it
Because the road was covered with silk
Because all traders had to wear silk clothes
28140.e: Silk from China was an expensive luxury in the West. The name Silk Road was only invented in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.
28140.m: The Silk Road is named after Chinese silk.

28141.q: Which parts of the world did the Silk Road link?
28141.e: The trade routes led from China through Central Asia to the Mediterranean. In the 2nd century BC the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian was one of the first to explore the lands in the West.
28141.m: The Silk Road linked China with the Mediterranean.

28142.q: Which feared desert did the caravans on the Silk Road have to go round to the north or south?
28142.e: The Taklamakan in the Tarim Basin is one of the largest sand deserts on Earth. The caravans travelled from oasis to oasis along its edges.
28142.m: The Silk Road led around the Taklamakan Desert.

28143.q: Which important oasis city on the Silk Road is in Uzbekistan today?
28143.e: Samarkand was a rich trading city of the Sogdians. Today, with its buildings, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
28143.m: Samarkand was an important stop on the Silk Road.

28144.q: Which sought-after goods did China under the Han get from the Fergana Valley?
28144.e: The Han wanted strong horses for their cavalry against the nomads. They were called “heavenly horses”.
28144.m: China got heavenly horses from Fergana via the Silk Road.

28145.q: How did goods usually travel along the whole of the Silk Road?
a: Passed on from trader to trader
28145.e: Hardly any trader travelled the whole way. The goods were sold on at markets and so taken step by step to the west or east.
28145.m: Goods on the Silk Road passed from trader to trader.

28146.q: Which religion came from India to China along the Silk Road?
28146.e: From the 1st century AD, monks and traders brought the Buddha’s teaching to China. Cave temples were built along the route.
28146.m: Buddhism came to China along the Silk Road.

28147.q: Which ancient people paid a lot of money for silk from China?
28147.e: In Rome, silk was an expensive luxury. The Romans only knew of China from hearsay and called the people there the Seres, meaning the silk people.
28147.m: The Romans bought expensive silk from China.

28148.q: In which modern country was the heartland of the Kingdom of Kush?
28148.e: Kush lay in Nubia on the middle Nile, south of Egypt. Most of this area is part of Sudan today.
28148.m: The Kingdom of Kush lay in today’s Sudan.

28149.q: What role did kings from Kush play in Egypt in the 8th and 7th centuries BC?
a: They built the Pyramid of Khufu
28149.e: The kings of Kush conquered Egypt and formed the 25th dynasty. They are often called the black pharaohs.
28149.m: Kings from Kush ruled Egypt as pharaohs.

28150.q: In which direction did the kings of Kush march to conquer Egypt?
28150.e: Kush lay south of Egypt. The kings marched with their armies down the Nile to the north and conquered Egypt around 730 BC.
